title: All 3D-Printed Conducting Polymer Hydrogel-Based Soft Surface Electromyography Electrode Array for Noninvasive Fatigue Assessment
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract High-density surface electromyography (sEMG) electrode arrays allow the recording of rich myoelectric signals and provide a useful approach for monitoring exercise-induced muscle fatigue. However, existing sEMG electrode arrays often suffer from mechanical mismatches between conventional rigid electrodes and soft tissues, as well as complex fabrication processes and limited programmability, which severely constrain the rational design and practical application of sEMG electrode arrays. Herein, we successfully fabricate an eight-channel PEDOT:PSS-PVA hydrogel-based soft sEMG electrode array via a multi-material 3D printing. Through systematic rheological characterization of the composite inks and rational design of a printable three-layer electrode architecture, we achieve seamless interfacial integration and integrated sequential fabrication. The as-prepared sEMG electrode array exhibits exceptional softness comparable to that of human soft tissues (Young’s modulus ∼ 10 kPa), low electrochemical impedance (∼22 Ω), and good electrochemical stability. Leveraging these advantageous properties, our sEMG electrode array enables noninvasive sEMG signal recording and monitoring of fatigue-associated sEMG changes with a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR > 20 dB) under various grip forces before and after exercise, and captures sEMG changes associated with fatigue progression during repetitive movements. These results validate the capability of our electrode array for high-quality sEMG monitoring of fatigue-associated electrophysiological features and open up promising avenues for future applications such as scientific athletic training.

title: Geometry-Driven Ultrahigh Current Density Field Emission from Vertically Oriented MXene Film Edge Emitters
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract MXenes are promising cold cathode materials owing to their high electrical conductivity, solution processability, and tunable surface terminations; however, realizing high-current-density field emission from MXene film emitters remains challenging because their planar two-dimensional geometry generally provides limited field concentration and restricts the number of field-activated emission sites. Here, we demonstrate a geometry-driven strategy to achieve high-current-density field emission from vertically oriented MXene film edge emitters. By systematically controlling the film height and inter-electrode gap, the optimized emitter achieves a current density of 5020 mA cm–2 at 1520 V, which is more than an order of magnitude higher than the values reported for previous MXene field emitters. Enhanced performance is not governed by the field enhancement factor alone. Instead, it is enabled by the balance between sufficient local field enhancement and a large effective emission area. Experimental Fowler–Nordheim analysis, emission pattern imaging, and the screening-corrected field-enhancement model indicate that excessive field concentration can promote edge-localized emission and reduce the effective emission area, whereas the optimized geometry enables distributed edge emission with improved stability. These findings establish edge-geometry engineering as a design principle for transforming two-dimensional MXene films into high-current-density cold cathodes for vacuum nanoelectronics.

title: Crystallinity-Dependent Donor Activation in RF-Sputtered SnO2 Electron-Transport Layers and the Interface-Character Origin of Their Predicted Device-Level Consequences
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract SnO2 is the electron-transport layer (ETL) in record n–i–p perovskite solar cells, grown by chemical bath deposition (CBD) without high-temperature crystallization; whether its crystallinity matters remains unresolved. Here, the same RF-sputtering process on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO), at room temperature or 300 °C, yields a predominantly amorphous or an FTO-templated polycrystalline rutile film. The measured film and interface properties anchor a calibrated TCAD model and a thirteen-parameter Sobol global sensitivity analysis (>33,000 simulations), which, unlike one-factor-at-a-time sweeps, resolves the interactions among parameters explicitly. At the film level, crystallinity governs donor activation: UPS, XPS, and STEM-EDS show that the amorphous film holds more fluorine yet has a Fermi level farther below the conduction band, so shallow donors attributed to substitutional fluorine exist in both films but are active only in the crystalline one. At the device level, however, the predicted gain arises from the crystalline film's interface rather than its doping. The Ag/SnO2 contact is rectifying on the amorphous film and ohmic on the crystalline one, through interface-state de-pinning rather than a band-offset shift. The Sobol analysis ranks the SnO2/perovskite interface trap density first (total-effect index ≈ 0.66). A degenerately doped film could screen such traps, but the amorphous film's rectification rules out that route; its deficit is interfacial. At its trap density (∼1013 cm–2), only deep acceptor-like states pin the Fermi level (acceptor-fraction index ≈ 0.83). The predicted crystallization gain is +5.6 pp (20.5 → 26.1%). FAPbI3 half-stack PL/TRPL supports this (1.35× longer lifetime on the crystalline ETL) and bounds that interface's trap density to ≲1012 cm–2. Crystalline growth is one route to the de-pinned interface that CBD ETLs reach chemically, provided that interface is preserved. The absolute efficiencies are calibrated predictions; the benefit's sign and the lever ranking are robust.

title: Dielectric Mie-Resonant Metasurface Integrated ATR Chip for Spectrally Tunable Surface-Enhanced Infrared Spectroscopy in Aqueous Media
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy provides label-free molecular fingerprints but often lacks sensitivity for trace analysis in aqueous media. Surface-enhanced infrared absorption (SEIRA) spectroscopy amplifies vibrational signals near nanostructured surfaces, yet conventional SEIRA platforms typically require sample drying, preconcentration, or noble metal substrates. Here, we introduce a monolithic all-silicon chip that integrates dielectric Mie-resonant micropillar arrays onto a microattenuated total reflection (µ-ATR) element using a complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible fabrication process. This µ-ATR SEIRA (µ-SEIRA) chip enables SEIRA directly in bulk aqueous media without sample drying, preconcentration, or noble metals. The µ-SEIRA chip provides spectrally tunable field enhancement, achieving a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.57 mM for aqueous sodium acetate, a 3.6-fold improvement over a flat silicon reference. Resonance tuning via the micropillar array geometry enables selective enhancement of specific vibrational bands, as demonstrated by the preferential enhancement of the Amide II band (∼1550 cm–1) over the Amide I band (∼1650 cm–1) in bovine serum albumin. The µ-SEIRA chip is low-cost, scalable, and disposable, reducing cross-contamination and throughput limitations associated with reusable ATR crystals for aqueous sample measurements.

title: Electrode-Side Catalytic Regulation Directs Electrolyte Decomposition for Stable Silicon Anodes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrochemical stability of silicon anodes is critically influenced by the initial decomposition pathways of fluorine-containing electrolyte species, which dictate the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) composition and stability. However, existing strategies primarily rely on electrolyte fluorination or artificial interphases to indirectly regulate SEI chemistry, whereas precise electrode-side regulation of fluorine-containing electrolyte decomposition remains challenging. Herein, a binder-free Co SACs-Si-N/C electrode is developed to direct interfacial reactions through single-atom catalysis. Atomically dispersed Co-N4 sites selectively strengthen PF6– adsorption, modulate the interfacial electronic structure, and steer fluorine-containing electrolyte species toward preferential inorganic decomposition, thereby constructing a compact LiF-rich SEI that suppresses parasitic reactions and stabilizes the silicon/electrolyte interface. As a result, the Co SACs-Si-N/C electrode delivers a reversible capacity of 1128.8 mAh g–1 after 1200 cycles at 1.0 A g–1, while lithium cobalt oxide pouch cells further demonstrate their practical applicability. Machine learning established a quantitative correlation between electrochemical characterization parameters and performance evolution. This work reveals the critical role of electrode-regulated interfacial reaction pathways in governing SEI evolution and provides a catalytic strategy for developing durable silicon-based anodes.

title: Peptide–DNA Hybrid Selection for Chemical Functionality Recognition across Diverse Material Interfaces
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Sequence-defined affinity ligands are powerful tools for molecular recognition, yet their selection has largely focused on defined molecular targets rather than shared chemical functionalities. Extending sequence-based recognition to a chemical moiety presents a distinct challenge because the same functionality must be recognized across structurally and chemically diverse molecular and material contexts. Here, we demonstrate that in vitro selection of peptide–DNA hybrids can generate an affinity ligand that recognizes a shared chemical functionality across distinct molecular and material interfaces. Using carboxylates as a model functionality, we selected a peptide–DNA hybrid library against a carboxylated material surface and identified R8rank1, whose enhanced binding depended on the selected DNA sequence functioning within the peptide–DNA hybrid architecture. R8rank1 hybrid preferentially recognized carboxylate-containing polymers with distinct molecular backbones over polymers bearing other functionalities, including an anionic sulfonate-containing polymer, and retained its recognition behavior across chemically distinct gold and silica nanoparticle interfaces presenting surface carboxylates. Fluorescently labeled R8rank1 further distinguished carboxylated from hydroxylated silica nanoparticles with an approximately eightfold difference in fluorescence and exhibited an apparent Kd of approximately 390 nM for the carboxylated surface, whereas the two surfaces were not significantly differentiated by zeta-potential measurements. This affinity-based readout provides chemical-functionality information complementary to conventional surface charge characterization. These findings extend sequence-based affinity selection from defined molecular targets to shared chemical functionalities and establish peptide–DNA hybrids as a selectable molecular recognition platform for identifying chemical functionalities across diverse material interfaces.

title: Selenium-Integrated MoO3 Composite Cathode for Rechargeable Magnesium Batteries
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Owing to their high volumetric capacity, potential for low-dendrite metal deposition, and abundance of natural magnesium, rechargeable magnesium batteries (RMBs) have garnered significant interest as potential substitutes for lithium-based systems. Nevertheless, sluggish Mg2+ diffusion and the polyselenide shuttle effect in selenium-based cathodes continue to restrict their practicality. In this work, a Se-MoO3 composite cathode was prepared by solvothermal synthesis of a MoSe2 precursor followed by annealing in air. Compact MoSe2 nanosheets were annealed to create an open hierarchical Se-MoO3 architecture composed of vertically oriented nanosheets associated with MoO3 nanoribbons. The Se-MoO3 cathode delivers 312 mAh g–1 at cycle 80 at 200 mA g–1. At 500 mA g–1, the capacity reaches 237 mAh g–1 at cycle 79 and decreases to 76.8 mAh g–1 at cycle 500. Ex situ measurements reveal reversible changes in the Mo and Se chemical states during cycling, supporting the participation of both components in charge storage. Although the close association between the Se-containing phase and MoO3 may influence the electrochemical response, the present data do not directly establish interface-specific polyselenide adsorption or catalytic conversion. Overall, this work emphasizes compositional and architectural modification as a viable approach for enhanced magnesium-ion storage.

title: Pneumatic Rigid-Soft Coupled Finger with Self-Powered Triboelectric Tactile Sensing toward Potential Application in Lunar Exploration
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Robotic manipulation in future lunar-surface operations and planetary sample-return missions requires end effectors capable of accommodating irregular objects while maintaining reliable tactile feedback under uncertain contact conditions. Motivated by these challenges, we present a terrestrial proof-of-concept of a pneumatic rigid–soft coupled robotic finger integrating structural regulation and self-powered triboelectric tactile sensing. The finger combines rigid skeletons, fiber-constrained pneumatic chambers, and a finger-pad sensing unit to enable compliant deformation, posture regulation, and tactile perception. A flexible single-electrode triboelectric sensor based on a PDMS-MXene composite generates electrical signals through contact electrification and electrostatic induction without external electrical excitation, while pneumatic actuation, signal acquisition, and computational processing require external power. At an input pressure of 140 kPa, the proximal interphalangeal, distal interphalangeal, and metacarpophalangeal regions achieved bending angles of approximately 84°, 76°, and 65°, respectively. The sensor exhibited stable outputs at contact frequencies of 1–10 Hz and a sensitivity of 0.11 V/kPa over 10–120 kPa. Incorporating 6 wt% MXene increased the output voltage by 50.8% compared with pure PDMS. Combined with a convolutional neural network-long short-term memory model, the system achieved classification accuracies of 97.6% for 10 representative laboratory materials and 99.5% for four surface-roughness levels under controlled terrestrial conditions. Grasping experiments further demonstrated compliant manipulation and tactile perception. These results establish the feasibility of the proposed sensing approach under laboratory conditions, while its applicability to planetary geological materials and space environments remains to be validated.

title: Engineering Ambipolar Charge Transport in Stable Solution-Processed Nanofilms of Electrically Conductive Liquid-Crystalline Anthraquinones
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The realization of ambipolar charge transport with long-term operational and environmental stability of the transport layer is a rarely addressed challenge in organic electronics, especially with respect to solution-processed devices. This study reports the molecular engineering of redox-active liquid-crystalline anthraquinones with triazole and cyanovinylene functional units to stabilize ordered columnar mesophases at room temperature. In addition to high thermal stability, solution-processed nanofilms of these discotic liquid crystals (DLCs) also demonstrate effective charge-extraction from injecting electrodes in diode devices, with their electrical conductivity values among the highest reported for DLC nanofilms (10–4 S/m). Alongside ultra-stable electrical performance over repeated electrical cycling, these devices exhibit long-term stability for up to two years without encapsulation under ambient storage conditions. Balanced ambipolarity is achieved via the fabrication of single-carrier devices where hole and electron mobilities both match at an order of 10–3 cm2/Vs. Being a pioneering report dedicated to detailed electrical conductivity studies and ambient stability of solution-processed ambipolar DLC films, the present work enriches the scope of practical DLC-based electronic devices from the fundamental viewpoint of molecular design.

title: Harmonized Na-Site Occupancy and Fe Local Structure in a Mixed-Phosphate Cathode for All-Climate Sodium-Ion Batteries
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7 (NFPP) has attracted considerable attention as a low-cost, structurally stable cathode for sodium-ion batteries. However, its commercialization is severely hampered by electrochemically inert impurities from conventional synthesis and insufficient energy density. Herein, we report a heteroatom-free strategy combining precursor pathway engineering with Na-site regulation and local Fe-environment modulation to synthesize a phase-pure NFPP-type cathode using a nominal Na3.67Fe2.67(PO4)1.67(P2O7) precursor stoichiometry. The resulting N3.67F2.67PP sample exhibits distinct Na-site occupancies from conventional NFPP. Theoretical calculations and experimental characterizations demonstrate that increased occupation ratios of Na4 and Na2 sites collectively elevate the discharge voltage plateau and enhance cycling stability. Meanwhile, precise regulation of the Na/Fe/PO4/P2O7 ratio modulates the electronic structure of Fe and increases Fe–O coordination disorder, markedly boosting Na+ migration kinetics and electronic conductivity. Consequently, the optimized material delivers a high specific capacity of 110.4 mAh g–1 at 0.1 C, retains 98.6% of its capacity after 1700 cycles at 1 C, and exhibits an impressive 103.5 mAh g–1 at 10 C. It also exhibits superior performance over a wide temperature range from –40 to 60 °C. Notably, Ah-level pouch and cylindrical batteries assembled with kilogram-scale materials achieve outstanding performance, highlighting a practical route toward commercialization. This work clarifies the structure–property relationship of NFPP-based materials and provides valuable guidance for designing high-performance mixed-phosphate cathodes.

title: Repurposing Grain Boundaries for Graphene Origami Auxetic Metamaterials with Enhanced Fatigue Resistance
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Graphene represents the pinnacle of intrinsic material strength, yet it remains functionally limited by a lack of plasticity and severe degradation in mechanical performance associated with porosity-driven upscaling. Although graphene origami (GOri) offers a deterministic alternative to porous networks, its realization has been restricted to chemically functionalized, metastable frameworks. Here, we demonstrate a computational design strategy that repurposes grain boundaries (GBs) observed in large-scale chemical vapor deposited (CVD) graphene as topological precursors for stable GOri structures. Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we show that periodic pentagon–heptagon (5–7) ring arrays within the tilted GBs can facilitate out-of-plane corrugations of the graphene domains, mimicking macroscopic folding creases without chemical modification. Our study also shows that the mechanical response of the proposed structure is highly tunable via linear grain size (µ) and dimensionless aspect ratio (α), enabling a wide range of control over tensile strength, elastic modulus, and negative Poisson’s ratio (NPR), reaching –3.77. Furthermore, the developed GB-GOri architecture achieves a 20% enhancement in fatigue strength and a fatigue life exceeding 150% of that of functionalized counterparts through pseudo-plastic deformation. Effectively, this GB-assisted defect engineering promotes stable crack growth and provides proof-of-concept for the future experimental fabrication of graphene-based auxetic metamaterials.

title: A cellular atlas of the preinvasive breast cancer microenvironment
abstract: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common preinvasive breast cancer, however our knowledge of the DCIS tumor microenvironment (TME) remains limited. We constructed a comprehensive atlas of the TME in estrogen-receptor positive DCIS using fresh samples collected from normal breast tissues, DCIS and invasive breast cancers. We analyzed 854,911 cells from 159 patients by single cell RNA sequencing and 39 samples by spatial transcriptomics, which identified 9 cell types and 60 cell states. Our data shows remodeling of fibroblasts, vascular and basal cells that encircle the DCIS regions and immunosuppressive ducts that support the growth of the preinvasive cancer cells. This study delineates early alterations in the DCIS TME, including many changes that persist during invasive progression.

title: Differentiation of stem-like CD4 + T cells modulates early effector responses in colorectal cancer
abstract: Strategies to improve cancer immunotherapy have largely focused on the intratumor immunosuppressive microenvironment, whereas approaches to amplify peripheral T cells and promote tumor recruitment have not been thoroughly explored. Using imaging mass cytometry in patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), we observed T helper 1 (T H 1)–like immune architectures in mismatch repair–deficient tumors associated with response to anti–programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) immunotherapy. By contrast, mismatch repair–proficient (pMMR) tumors showed regulatory T–dominant spatial interactions. Clonal analyses revealed that stem-like CD4 + T cells differentiated into T H 1-like cells after PD-1 blockade. In pMMR CRC mouse models, combined OX40 agonist and PD-1 blockade suppressed tumor progression by expanding Il7r + early effector CD4 + intermediates in tumor-draining lymph nodes, promoting migration and connection with T H 1-like cells. This was accompanied by interferon-γ–dependent induction of immunostimulatory monocyte-macrophages and CD8 + effector T cells. These findings suggest that leveraging peripheral CD4 + T cell amplification may improve immunotherapy responses.

title: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
abstract: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Twist angle, pressure, and strain directly modify the lattice and thus act as highly effective tuning parameters. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. In selected doping regimes, the elastoresistance exhibited a Curie-Weiss–like temperature divergence. We discuss possible microscopic origins, including nematic fluctuations and enhanced electronic entropy from fluctuating isospin moments. Our work establishes uniaxial strain as a versatile probe of correlated physics in a moiré material.

title: Direct monitoring of breaching in deltaic submarine landslides
abstract: Submarine landslides threaten seabed infrastructure and trigger the transport of globally important amounts of sediment, carbon, and pollutants to deep-sea environments. However, fully submarine landslides have never been directly monitored in nature. Past hypotheses for their failure mechanism and dynamics therefore remain unvalidated for natural settings, including that prolonged upslope-migrating failures (breaching) occur in sandy seafloor environments. In this work, we present direct underwater monitoring of fully submarine landslides at Homathko Delta in western Canada that retrogress slowly upslope, indicating breaching-type failure. Their prolonged rather than instantaneous nature has important implications for the stress that seabed structures must be designed to withstand. Prolonged landslides also initiate sustained sediment flows (turbidity currents) that efficiently transport sediment, carbon, and pollutants further offshore.

title: Tracking danger on the peaks
abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

title: Antiferroelectric hafnia down to the 2D limit
abstract: Antiferroelectricity is a material property characterized by alternating electric dipoles spontaneously ordered in antiparallel directions. Antiferroelectrics are promising for energy storage, solid-state cooling, and memory technologies; however, these materials are scarce, and their scalability remains largely unexplored. In this work, we demonstrated that single-crystalline hafnia, a lead-free complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS)–compatible material, exhibits antiferroelectricity under compressive-strain conditions. We observed antiparallel sublattice polarization and stable double hysteresis in single-crystalline (111)-oriented epitaxial lanthanum (La)–doped hafnia films grown on yttrium-stabilized zirconia and showed that the antipolar orthorhombic phase of hafnia adheres to the Kittel model of antiferroelectricity. Compressive strain strengthens the orthorhombic order in thinner La-doped hafnia films, achieving a very high ordering temperature of 850°C in the two-dimensional limit, highlighting hafnia’s potential for advanced antiferroelectric devices.

title: Conjugate Chiral Carbon Dots for Scalable Asymmetric Photocatalysis in Flow
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Carbon dots (CDs) have emerged as scalable, metal-free photocatalysts, but their use as conjugate organo-photocatalysts for enantioselective chemistry remains unexplored. Here, we covalently anchor a chiral imidazolidinone organocatalyst to amorphous, citric acid-derived CDs, giving a colloidal conjugate that acts as both photosensitizer and enantiodetermining component. This chiral CD material promotes the asymmetric radical α-alkylation of aldehydes in up to 84% yield and 93% e.e. Its semihomogeneous nature enables catalyst recovery by precipitation and reuse over five cycles with only minor loss in yield and e.e. The well-dispersed conjugate is also compatible with continuous photoflow, where Bayesian optimization in only 10 experiments enabled a gram-scale reaction in 80% yield and 91% e.e. This work establishes chiral conjugate CDs as a practical, recoverable platform for sustainable asymmetric photocatalysis.

title: A Multimetallic Single-Atom Catalyst on a Defective Graphene Support toward Methanol Oxidation and Oxygen Reduction Reactions: Density Functional Theory, Machine Learning, and Experiments
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Multimetallic single-atom catalysts (SACs) have emerged as promising candidates for electrocatalytic reactions. However, identifying bifunctional multimetallic SACs capable of efficiently catalyzing both the oxygen reduction and methanol oxidation reactions (ORR and MOR), applicable to direct methanol fuel cells, remains challenging due to the vast compositional design space. Here, we propose a defective graphene-supported multimetallic SAC (M1M2M3M4M5-SAC) incorporating Mn, Pt, Fe, Ni, Co, and Cu for simultaneous MOR and ORR catalysis. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations along with machine learning (ML) predictions reveal that the Co active site in PtFeNiCoCu-SAC delivers the most favorable performance, exhibiting ORR and MOR overpotentials of 0.47 and 0.46 V, respectively. Guided by these insights, we synthesized PtFeNiCoCu-SAC and a nitrogen-doped sample, confirming their atomic structures using X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). Electrochemical measurements validate the theoretical predictions: PtFeNiCoCu-SAC achieves an experimental ORR overpotential of 0.30 VRHE and a Tafel slope of 114 mV/dec at –1 mA/cm2, along with a half-wave potential of 0.86 VRHE. This catalyst also demonstrates good MOR activity, with a pronounced oxidation peak at 0.97 VRHE. Therefore, this work establishes a DFT- and ML-guided strategy for the accelerated rational design of multimetallic SACs and highlights PtFeNiCoCu-SAC as a promising bifunctional catalyst for energy-conversion applications.

title: n -Value-Tuned Quasi-2D Perovskites for Wavelength-Selective Optoelectronic Synapses
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Neuromorphic vision systems demand optoelectronic synapses that combine wavelength-selective sensing with gradual and linear synaptic weight updates. In two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites, extending visible-light absorption can be accompanied by accelerating ion migration and premature current saturation. Here, we regulate the phase composition of quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) BA2MA(n–1)PbnI(3n+1) perovskites by tuning the nominal n value. Incorporation of the n = 2 phase extends the absorption edge from 525 nm (green) to approximately 600 nm (red), enabling distinguishable responses under blue, green, and red illumination. The nominal n = 1.2 composition provides sufficient higher-n phase for red-light absorption while suppressing excessive ion migration, yielding highly linear photocurrent weight updates. Using these wavelength-, intensity-, and duration-dependent responses, we construct a light-history regression model that maps accumulated exposure to electrical blue-light-hazard warning and literature-derived phototoxicity thresholds under different color temperatures. This phase-engineering strategy provides a material-level route to integrate spectral selectivity and linear signal integration in neuromorphic vision systems.

title: Integrated 3D Porous Copper@BiSb Alloy Anodes via Pulse Electrodeposition for High-Performance Potassium-Ion Storage
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Antimony (Sb) and bismuth (Bi) are promising alloy-type anode materials for potassium-ion batteries (PIBs), yet Sb suffers from a massive 390% volume expansion during potassiation, while Bi is limited by a relatively low specific capacity of 384 mAh·g–1. Moreover, existing synthesis methods for BiSb alloys are complex, costly, and require binders or conductive additives that impair electrochemical performance. Herein, we innovatively fabricate an integrated 3D porous copper@BiSb (3DPC@BiSb) electrode by pulse electrodepositing BiSb alloy onto a 3D porous copper (3DPC) substrate. The 3DPC scaffold provides abundant active sites, shortens ion diffusion pathways, and mitigates volume expansion, while the binder-free design eliminates interfacial issues. Electrochemical tests demonstrate that the 3DPC@BiSb electrode delivers a reversible capacity of 400.6 mAh·g–1 at 0.1 A·g–1 after 100 cycles and retains 205.0 mAh·g–1 even at 32 C, outperforming most reported alloy-type anodes for PIBs. Kinetic analysis, ex-situ X-ray diffraction, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the superior performance originates from the synergistic effect of Sb (high capacity) and Bi (structural stability), enhanced K+ adsorption energy, and reduced diffusion barrier. This work provides a scalable strategy for fabricating integrated alloy anodes capable of large-area electrode preparation. It offers insights into the structure-performance relationship of BiSb-based materials, advancing the development of high-performance thin-film PIBs for renewable energy storage.

title: A Repeatable Supramolecular Adhesive with Ultrastrong Underwater Adhesion, Self-Healing Ability, and Long-Term Stability
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Repeatable adhesives attract enormous attention for their environmental friendliness and adaptability but suffer from weak adhesion when used in underwater conditions. Herein, we develop a supramolecular adhesive by incorporating quadruple hydrogen-bonded units into isocyanate-modified polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) polymers. By synergistically utilizing interfacial covalent bonds and multiple hydrogen bonds, the supramolecular adhesive exhibits repeatable adhesion in air for at least 5 cycles and ultrastrong underwater adhesion of ∼9.37 MPa. The rapid establishment of covalent bonds on various substrate surfaces confers the adhesive with instantaneous and tough adhesion in both air and underwater environments. Reversible multiple hydrogen bonds within the adhesive polymers endow the material with self-healing performance. In addition, rheology analysis combined with mechanical tests revealed the thermal-responsive property of the adhesive. Taking advantage of the self-healing performance and thermal-responsive adhesion, the adhesive exhibits repeatable ability. This work deepens the understanding of multiple hydrogen bonds and isocyanate-modified PDMS polymers, enabling the fabrication of repeatable adhesives for industrial applications.

title: Strain Gradient Engineering at Material Interfaces: Flexocatalysis Beyond Centrosymmetry
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The flexoelectric effect, an electromechanical coupling phenomenon ubiquitous in all materials (including centrosymmetric crystals) under non-uniform strain gradients, has recently given rise to the emerging field of flexocatalysis. By eliminating the need for external light or electrical biases and circumventing the symmetry constraints of piezoelectric materials, it represents a catalytic paradigm for green chemistry, with applications spanning water splitting for hydrogen production, hydrogen peroxide generation, pollutant degradation, and biomedical therapies (e.g., tumor treatment). This review systematically outlines the fundamentals of the flexoelectric effect and the strain gradient-driven charge separation mechanisms. Recent advances in representative applications across energy, environmental, and biomedical fields are comprehensively summarized. Additionally, preliminary strategies to enhance catalytic efficiency are categorized into two main approaches: (1) amplifying the flexoelectric response, primarily interface engineering, the synergistic coupling of piezoelectric and flexoelectric effects, and doping; and (2) optimizing charge separation and transfer, mainly via introduction of vacancies, photo-flexoelectric synergistic coupling, and single-atom modification. Finally, the current challenges and future opportunities of flexocatalysis are highlighted, providing a foundational roadmap that bridges solid-state physics and interfacial catalysis.

title: Room-Temperature Phosphorescent Materials Based on β-Diketone Derivatives Exhibiting Excitation- & Concentration-Dependent Characteristics
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) materials have attracted extensive attention owing to their potential applications in chemical sensing, optoelectronic devices, bioimaging, and information encryption. However, developing RTP materials with dynamically tunable emission colors that respond to multiple external stimuli remains a significant challenge. In this work, BA@TTA composites were constructed by doping 2-thenoyltrifluoroacetone (TTA) guest molecules into a boric acid (BA) host matrix, exhibiting efficient room-temperature afterglow. Upon changing the excitation wavelength from 254 nm to 365 nm, the afterglow emission color can be tuned from blue to yellow, indicating prominent excitation-wavelength-dependent luminescence behavior. Moreover, with increasing TTA content, the yellow afterglow under 365 nm excitation is gradually enhanced, whereas the blue afterglow component under 254 nm excitation remains nearly unchanged. This excitation- & concentration-dependent color-tunable phosphorescence of BA@TTA originates from the coexistence of isolated and aggregated TTA species, in which efficient intermolecular energy transfer and aggregation-induced electronic interactions reduce the excited-state energy gap, enhance spin–orbit coupling, and accelerate intersystem crossing, thereby enabling color-tunable room-temperature phosphorescence. This universal mechanism is extended to other β-diketone derivatives for high-security multi-level information encryption.

title: Berberine/Verteporfin Nanomicelles Enable O2-Economized Photodynamic Immunotherapy in Esophageal Cancer Via Tumor Metabolic Remodeling
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Photodynamic therapy (PDT) can convert oxidative damage into systemic antitumor immunity, but mitochondrial oxygen consumption, lactate accumulation, and aberrant angiogenesis create a hypoxic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that limits treatment. Here, berberine (BBR) and verteporfin (VER) were co-loaded into nanomicelles (BV NMs) through sonication-assisted self-assembly of PEG-g-(PVAc-co-PVCL), creating a “microenvironment remodeling—PDT potentiation—immune activation” strategy. BV NMs had a hydrodynamic diameter of 56.15 ± 0.30 nm. Drug loading lowered the critical micelle concentration from 11.2 μg/mL (blank micelles) to an apparent 1.3 μg/mL (BV NMs), supporting dilution stability. It also enhanced aqueous dispersibility, cellular uptake, and intratumoral accumulation. Mechanistically, BBR reduced mitochondrial complex I-associated activity, intracellular adenosine triphosphate levels, and extracellular lactate accumulation, attenuated cellular hypoxia and hypoxia-inducible factor-1α responses, and increased intracellular oxygen availability. Before irradiation, VER suppressed Yes-associated protein signaling and vascular endothelial growth factor expression, providing light-independent antitumor and antiangiogenic regulation. Under 660 nm irradiation, VER induced reactive oxygen species accumulation, mitochondrial depolarization, tumor-cell death, and immunogenic cell death. In vivo, BV NMs combined with irradiation achieved an approximately 96% inhibition rate based on terminal tumor weight. Proportions of mature dendritic cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes and splenic CD8+ T cells reached 3.33 and 2.73 times the control levels, respectively, alongside expansion of memory CD8+ T-cell populations. Treatment also reduced experimental pulmonary metastatic burden, achieved 50% survival at day 60, and caused no evident short-term systemic toxicity. This platform couples metabolic and angiogenic regulation with oxygen-dependent PDT and antitumor immunity, providing a strategy against primary and metastatic tumors.

title: Photoelectrochemical CO2 Reduction to CO by a Molecular Catalyst Attached to Pyrene-Terminated Silicon through Noncovalent Interactions
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract A ruthenium-based CO2 reduction catalyst immobilized on a Si photocathode through noncovalent π–π interactions is active for the photochemical conversion of CO2 to CO, with 34% ± 20% Faradaic efficiency with current densities of j = –(0.3 ± 0.1) mA cm–2 at –1.9 V vs Fc+/0 in an acetonitrile/water electrolyte solution under 1 sun illumination. Si photocathodes were functionalized with pyrene (p-Si–Py) using a Grignard methodology. A previously reported CO2 reduction catalyst, [Ru(tpy)(Mebim-py)(NCCH3)][PF6]2 (tpy = 2,2′:6′,2″-terpyridine, Mebim-py = 1-methylbenzimidazol-2-ylidene-3-(2′-pyridine)) was modified to include a pyrene moiety in the terpyridine backbone, enabling π–π stacking of the catalyst onto the Si surface to achieve a surface coverage of (1.85 ± 0.28) x 10–12 mol cm–2 (ca. 2% to 5% of a monolayer) as quantified via inductively coupled plasma mass spectroscopy (ICP-MS). A 420 mV photovoltage (Vph) was quantified for the p-Si–Py photocathode. Measurements of charge carrier recombination kinetics through time-resolved infrared spectroscopy indicate that surface attachment of pyrene moieties introduces defects at the Si interface, even without the presence of the catalyst. These defects provide competing kinetic pathways for photogenerated carriers, hypothesized to influence the selectivity of the hybrid photoelectrode, an important implication for future designs of hybrid photoelectrodes.

title: Reticular Materials as Optical Sensors of Volatile Organic Compounds for Healthcare and Environmental Monitoring
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are a family of molecules that possess high vapor pressure and are regarded as air pollutants that prevail in both indoor and outdoor settings. Prolonged exposure to VOCs poses a serious risk to human health. On the other hand, VOCs emitted by humans and plants have been recognized as key biomarkers to estimate the status of health and physiology in living beings. Profiling the total content of VOCs in human and plant fluids leads to early diagnosis of diseases and timely treatment. Monitoring the presence of VOCs, either to track air pollution or to estimate the status of health, has therefore commanded increasing attention. Among the various techniques, optical sensing methods have been sought after owing to the considerations of their fast response time, versatility, miniaturization and portability, as well as the possibility of performing non-invasive detection. Advanced functional materials, such as porous reticular solids, including metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), covalent organic frameworks (COFs), and hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs), are well suited not only as sorbents for the detection and capture of VOCs but also as suitable substrates for various approaches of optical signaling. This review, through recent case studies, presents the advances in the optical sensing of VOCs by reticular materials. In addition, a comparative analysis between various reticular material types has been provided, along with an outline of the current challenges and the opportunities that exist for future research.

title: Microfluidic Control of Biomolecular Condensate Growth Reveals Scaling Crossover and Interfacial Regulation
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Biomolecular condensates, formed via phase separation, play vital roles in cellular organization, yet their nucleation and growth dynamics remain poorly understood, particularly under controlled physiological conditions. Here, we employ a microfluidic platform to precisely manipulate the nucleation and growth of PGL-3 protein condensates at fluid–solid interfaces. We demonstrate that ionic strength and co-phase-separating proteins (SEPA-1) robustly tune the nucleation rate without altering the long-term growth scaling ∼tn. Single-condensate tracking further resolves a dynamic scaling crossover from rapid isolated growth with n ≃ 1/2 to diffusion-limited collective growth with n ≃ 1/3, consistent with simulations of overlapping protein-depletion fields. Furthermore, we show that this classical scaling breaks down during viscoelastic phase separation, where elastic-dominated condensates exhibit a significantly reduced exponent. Our work establishes molecular modulation and interfacial mechanics as key regulators of condensate dynamics, revealing physical principles that govern the size and material state of biological condensates.

title: Epigenetic gatekeeping enables genome-scale horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic cells
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer drives rapid evolutionary innovation, yet well-substantiated cases are largely confined to prokaryotes. Eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfer remains exceptionally rare, and direct genome-scale demonstrations are absent. Here, inspired by endosymbiotic genome acquisition, we show that mammalian cells can initiate genome-scale horizontal gene transfer through phagocytic uptake of intact algal cells, albeit at a much lower frequency than cell fusion. Live-cell imaging captures the early nuclear appearance of transferred algal DNA after fusion, while genome sequencing and cytogenetic analyses reveal stable retention of chromosome-scale algal DNA in mammalian cells. Hybrid cells maintain more than 16 Mb of algal DNA, including intact chromosomes, as telomere-linked structures that persist for 95 generations without selection. Transferred algal DNA shows a progressive increase in DNA methylation together with enrichment of repressive histone modifications, forming heterochromatic domains that physically associate with host chromosomes. Notably, mammalian cells deficient in a de novo DNA methyltransferase show reduced stable establishment and retention of transferred algal DNA, supporting a gatekeeping role for DNA methylation in the stable accommodation of foreign genomes. Our findings reveal an epigenetic mechanism that contributes to the stable accommodation of large-scale foreign DNA between distantly related eukaryotes.

title: Specific Amino Acid Imaging of Protein Condensates in Live Cells by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Intracellular protein condensates formed by liquid–liquid phase separation have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their key roles in many physiological and pathological processes. However, fluorescence imaging of protein condensates is limited by the bulky fluorescent tags that could perturb the protein localization and interaction. Imaging techniques that can visualize protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbations remain lacking. Here, we develop a strategy to image intracellular protein condensates by coupling stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy to specific amino acid labeling. Different types of amino acids are found to exhibit distinct incorporation patterns in the live cells. By metabolic labeling of deuterated tyrosine-d4 and arginine-d7, ALS-related fused in sarcoma (FUS) protein condensates can be visualized with a high specificity. In addition, two-color pulse-chase imaging reveals protein translation arrest in FUS condensates under stress conditions. Furthermore, heterogeneous tyrosine phosphorylation is imaged in live cells and FUS condensates based on the Raman blue shift of phosphorylated tyrosine-d4. Thus, our technique to image specific amino acids by SRS provides a new platform to visualize the metabolic turnover and post-translational modifications of protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbation.

title: Visible-Light-Driven Dearomatization via Electrocyclic Ring Expansion for Solar Energy Storage
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage compounds capture solar photon energy in the strained chemical bonds of metastable photoisomers and release it on demand as heat, yet simultaneously achieving visible-light absorption and high energy storage density has remained a persistent challenge. Here we introduce 9-aryl acridine N-oxides as MOST compounds based on visible-light-driven dearomative ring expansion. Irradiation at 470 nm, near the solar irradiance maximum at 482 nm, quantitatively converts these compounds to metastable 1,2-oxazepines, which thermally revert to the parent N-oxides and discharge the stored energy. The system achieves energy storage densities of up to 0.54 MJ/kg, comparable to Dewar anthracenes, while absorbing substantially more red-shifted light and offering nearly 3 orders of magnitude longer storage lifetimes of up to 1.4 years in the solid state. The thermal half-lives of the 1,2-oxazepines are tunable through para-substitution on the aryl ring and solvation, enabling up to a 1,300-fold reduction in half-life. Crucially, the 9-aryl substituent biases the transient oxaziridine intermediate toward selective reversion to the N-oxide over competing decomposition pathways, overcoming the limitations of other acridine N-oxides reported to date. This work establishes light-induced ring expansion as an effective strategy for MOST and expands the scope of viable MOST compounds.

title: Photomediated Chromium-Catalyzed Regio-, Diastereo-, and Enantioselective Deoxygenative Coupling of Activated Allylic and Propargylic Alcohols with Aldehydes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Chromium-catalyzed asymmetric Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction is a powerful tool for constructing synthetically valuable enantioenriched homoallylic alcohols and allenols. However, catalytic asymmetric NHK-type coupling of allylic or propargylic C–O electrophiles remains largely underdeveloped. Herein, we report a photomediated chromium-catalyzed deoxygenative coupling of activated allylic and propargylic alcohols with aldehydes, enabling the synthesis of a variety of chiral homoallylic alcohols with wide structural diversity and allenols. The reactions were performed under mild conditions, and a wide range of synthetically useful functional groups was found to be well tolerated. Importantly, this method provides a straightforward way for the construction of homoallylic alcohols bearing a chiral quaternary carbon center with high ee and dr. Furthermore, stereodivergent access to all four homoallylic alcohol stereoisomers is realized through orthogonal combinations of Z/E-configured allylic alcohols and R/S-configured ligands. Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies provided insight into the key catalytic intermediate and the origin of stereocontrol.

title: Hybrid Weakly Coordinated Solvents for Fast-Charging and Wide-Temperature Sodium-Ion Full Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The application of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) in wide-temperature and fast-charging scenarios is severely constrained by the performance limitations of electrolytes. Conventional ester-based electrolytes struggle to simultaneously achieve high ionic conductivity, low desolvation energy, and excellent interfacial stability. Herein, we propose a hybrid solvent system comprising ethyl propionate and ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN), aiming to synergistically enhance the rate capability and temperature adaptability of SIBs. The relatively weak coordination ability of both solvents effectively promotes anion participation in solvation structure, significantly lowering the Na+ desolvation energy barrier and inducing the formation of stable, inorganic-rich electrode/electrolyte interphases. Meanwhile, the dual-solvent combination increases the diversity of solvation configurations and reduces ion clustering, thereby enhancing ionic conductivity. The intrinsic nonflammability and excellent film-forming ability of PFPN further enhance safety and synergistically strengthen interfacial stability. Therefore, Prussian blue||hard carbon full cells operate stably over a wide temperature range from −50 to 100 °C. Notably, ampere-hour-level pouch cells deliver a capacity retention of 86.3% after 300 cycles at 25 °C and maintain stable operation for over 100 cycles even at −20 and 80 °C. This solvent synergy strategy offers a practical new pathway for the development of electrolytes for SIBs in extreme environments.

title: Functional Specialization of Coordination Spheres Enables Site-Selective Aromatic C–H Isotope Exchange in Ni Single-Atom Catalysts
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Engineering single-atom catalysts has predominantly focused on tailoring the primary coordination sphere, whereas whether distinct coordination spheres can be endowed with independent catalytic functions remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the functional specialization of coordination spheres by constructing a phosphorus-modified Ni–N2O2 single-atom catalyst for site-selective C–H deuteration. Advanced spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations show that phosphorus is incorporated outside the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination environment and support an O-linked phosphorus environment as a preferential second-sphere motif. This architecture decouples substrate recognition from catalytic activation. Specifically, second-sphere phosphorus selectively recognizes and anchors the amino group of haloanilines to dictate deuteration site selectivity, whereas the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination sphere promotes H2 activation and undergoes H2-assisted regeneration following D2O-induced hydroxylation, facilitated by P–O–Ni electronic communication, thereby sustaining efficient catalytic turnover. Consequently, the catalyst achieves highly site-selective C–H deuteration of chloro-, bromo-, and iodoanilines using H2 and D2O while completely preserving carbon–halogen bonds, whereas the phosphorus-free analogue exhibits negligible activity. This work identifies the structural origin and catalytic function of second-sphere phosphorus and establishes functional specialization of coordination spheres as a general design principle for independently programming substrate recognition and catalytic turnover in single-atom catalysis.

title: Magnetic Resonance Silent Activatable Probe with Massive Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated Fibrogenesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Biomarker-specific molecular imaging is vital in precision medicine. However, a fundamental challenge of most molecular imaging methods is the difficulty of distinguishing specific molecular signal from nonspecific signal arising from the distribution of the molecular probe. This is even more pronounced in metabolically active organs such as the kidney and liver where the probe may concentrate prior to elimination. As a result, almost all molecular imaging relies on delayed imaging to achieve specificity, but this constrains clinical throughput and impedes rapid assessment of the diseased organ. Here, we report a magnetic resonance (MR) probe, Fe(II)-IAFP2, which combines 3 drivers of relaxivity enhancement to decouple disease specificity from probe distribution. Fe(II)-IAFP2 is MR-silent in its Fe(II) state, producing negligible MR signal even at high concentrations. In inflammatory, fibrogenic microenvironments common to many diseases, rapid oxidation to Fe(III) activates MR enhancement, while reversible aldehyde-mediated binding to remodeled extracellular matrix further amplifies relaxivity and promotes retention at the site of tissue injury. This dual activation–retention mechanism enables robust signal generation within minutes of administration. In mouse models of renal and liver fibrogenesis, Fe(II)-IAFP2 generated disease-associated MR contrast within minutes after intravenous administration. Together, this work demonstrates an effective strategy for rapid, activity-based molecular MR imaging through the combination of pathological activation and complementary tissue retention.

title: Ammonia-Driven Nanoscale Surface Restructuring of Copper Catalysts during Nitrate Reduction Reaction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrolyte and applied potential are known to impact a catalyst’s structure and performance, yet the role of reaction intermediates and products in driving surface evolution remains largely unexplored. Here, using electrochemical atomic force microscopy, we show that the dynamic restructuring of copper (Cu) surfaces during nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) directly correlates with the rate and selectivity of ammonia (NH3) formation. At moderate overpotentials, where nitrite formation dominates, lateral expansion of Cu terraces is observed, whereas rapid NH3 formation at higher cathodic potentials induces Cu adislands enriched in low-coordinated step sites, revealing distinct restructuring pathways that accompany the transition from nitrite- to ammonia-selective NO3RR. These transformations are rationalized by an NH3-mediated Cu dissolution-redeposition mechanism. Our results identify reaction products as active modulators of catalyst surface structure, establishing a framework for understanding reaction-driven catalyst restructuring and enabling in situ control of catalyst surfaces through the interfacial reaction environment.

title: Acetaldehyde-Mediated Direct Conversion of Air to Nitric Acid
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The sustainable synthesis of nitric acid (HNO3) directly from air via N2 oxidation is a dream reaction but remains a long-standing challenge, owing to formidable thermodynamic and kinetic barriers. Here, we report a photoassisted thermocatalytic strategy in which acetaldehyde as a key medium enables efficient N2 oxidation to HNO3 under mild conditions. Acetaldehyde is oxidized to peracetic acid over 316L stainless steel, which subsequently generates radicals (CH3COOO•) under visible-light irradiation. These CH3COOO• radicals are highly reactive and can oxidize N2 at 200 °C and near-ambient pressures (1–5 bar), affording an HNO3 formation rate of 110.8 μmol h–1 with a concentration of 13,961 ppm and an N2 conversion of 0.45% within 2 h─approximately 2 to 4 orders of magnitude higher than previously reported systems. Notably, the kinetic irrelevance of H2O enables operation in a gas-phase flow configuration, allowing continuous and stable HNO3 production and gram-scale accumulation at the laboratory scale. This work introduces a groundbreaking reaction paradigm that couples organic radical chemistry and surface catalysis, offering a scalable and energy-efficient pathway for the green synthesis of HNO3.

title: A Molybdoenzyme Mediates Carbon–Sulfur Bond Making and Breaking in Ergothioneine Biosynthesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The molybdopterin-dependent ergothioneine synthase (MES) from Caldithrix abyssi is the first molybdoenzyme known to catalyze the formation of carbon–sulfur bonds. To complete its catalytic cycle, this bifunctional enzyme desulfurates l-cysteine at a pyridoxal 5′-phosphate binding site and transfers the harvested sulfur atom (S0) to the molybdenum center of a bis-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide cofactor more than 50 Å away. Subsequently, the sulfurated Mo-center transfers the labile sulfur atom onto the imidazole ring of Nα-trimethyl histidine (TMH). Combining experimental observations from cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, sequence-activity correlation, and substrate-specificity studies, we delineate the structural basis for long-distance sulfur transfer via a persulfide relay, the identity of the imidazole sulfurating species, and key sequence motifs that are indispensable for activity. Furthermore, the reversibility of MES-mediated sulfurization of TMH under physiological conditions suggests that ergothioneine may serve as a soluble reservoir of oxidizing equivalents, supporting anaerobic metabolism in deep-branching bacteria such as C. abyssi.

title: Empowering HFIP as a Radical Trifluoromethylating Reagent by Photoelectrochemical Iron Catalysis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The development of practical synthetic methods for incorporating trifluoromethyl (CF3) groups into organic scaffolds is of paramount importance in medicinal chemistry, as such modifications profoundly modulate the physicochemical properties of drug candidates. 1,1,1,3,3,3-Hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP) is widely utilized as a unique solvent in synthetic chemistry and also represents a promising CF3 source due to its high availability and low cost. Here we report an unprecedented photoelectrochemical iron-catalyzed protocol for radical trifluoromethylation that employs commercially accessible HFIP as the CF3 radical precursor. This method enables efficient trifluoromethylation of unactivated arenes, heteroarenes, and alkenes with a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance. Notably, this photoelectrocatalytic system is readily scalable for practical synthetic applications, and its utility has been demonstrated in the trifluoromethylation of peptides, allowing preferential modification of tryptophan residues in a chemoselective fashion.

title: General Synthesis of Functionalized 1,3-Diamines from Azoarenes and Enoates via Electrochemical Annulation and N–N Bond Cleavage Followed by Chemical Reduction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Despite the widespread utility of N-substituted 1,3-diamines across numerous fields, their selective synthesis directly from readily available feedstocks remains a long-standing challenge. In this context, we report a room-temperature electrochemical protocol for the synthesis of both symmetrical and unsymmetrical N,N′-disubstituted 1,3-diamines through electrochemical transformation of azoarenes with enoates, followed by convergent reduction of the resulting β-amino amides. This method features broad substrate scope, operational simplicity, no need for noble transition-metal catalysts, and high chemoselectivity. Mechanistic studies indicate that the reaction is initiated by the reduction of azoarenes, facilitated by HCOOH, while Zn2+ ions leached from anodic oxidation serve as a Lewis acid to promote intramolecular cyclization via ester amidation. Subsequent cathodic reduction drives N–N bond cleavage to afford the β-amino amide intermediates, thereby endowing azoarenes with dual-nitrogen synthon capability. This work provides a practical platform for the general synthesis of N,N′-difunctionalized 1,3-diamines and convenient late-stage structural editing of biomedicals.

title: Linker Steric Hindrance-Induced Defect Engineering Enables Oxygen Vacancy-Rich MOFs for Pollutant Degradation
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The widespread contamination of water by emerging contaminants (ECs) demands the development of efficient remediation technologies. Although advanced oxidation processes reliant on reactive oxygen species (ROS) show promise, they typically depend on energy- or reagent-intensive activation methods. Here, we introduce a linker steric hindrance-induced defect engineering (LSH-DE) strategy for metal–organic frameworks, which enables catalytic ROS generation using molecular oxygen (O2) as a benign terminal oxidant at ambient temperature and pressure. By systematically modulating the steric bulk of organic linkers, we precisely create missing-linker defects and direct the formation of oxygen vacancy (Vo) in robust Ce-UiO-66 during a rapid 15 min synthesis. Spectroscopic and computational analyses confirm that these oxygen vacancies promote O2 adsorption and activation to yield superoxide radicals (•O2–). The optimized catalyst, Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2, demonstrates superior activity in degrading ubiquitous ECs without requiring external energy inputs or chemical mediators. Furthermore, integration of Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2 into a membrane-based recirculating flow-through system enabled sustained water treatment, maintaining >90% BPA removal over 48 h with a high water permeance of 101.5 L m–2 h–1 bar–1. This work presents a general and sustainable approach for designing catalytic defects in MOFs, advancing the development of green, next-generation water purification technologies.

title: Breaking the “Micro-Size Inversion” Paradox via a Surface-Chemistry-Driven Molecular Sieving Membrane for Ambient Lithium–Air Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Lithium–air batteries suffer from moisture-induced parasitic reactions and electrolyte evaporation in ambient air. A fundamental challenge is the “micro-size inversion” paradox, where H2O (0.275 nm) is smaller than O2 (0.346 nm), rendering conventional size-based sieving ineffective. Here, we report a composite membrane composed of polydimethylsiloxane and fluorinated vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-VF) to break this selectivity barrier. By grafting 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyl groups onto a vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-V), we establish a surface-chemistry-driven sieving mechanism. This design creates a molecular-level hydrogen-bond-repellent barrier that specifically inhibits polar H2O penetration while maintaining high nonpolar O2 flux, effectively decoupling the permeability-hydrophobicity trade-off. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborate this mechanism, demonstrating that the COF-VF exhibits significantly reduced adsorption affinity toward H2O compared to the pristine COF-V. In 40% RH ambient air, the battery equipped with this membrane delivers a discharge capacity of 3596 mAh g–1 and sustains cycling for 2700 h (270 cycles), a 10.8-fold improvement over unprotected cells. Advanced characterizations via DRT and DEMS confirm that the membrane promotes reversible Li2O2 formation and significantly suppresses LiOH accumulation. This work provides a multiscale strategy for molecular-level selective separation in practical energy storage.

title: A Double-Tethered Metallacyclobutadiene Catalyst for Cyclic Polymer Synthesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The synthesis, characterization, and catalytic polymerization results of an unprecedented double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complex (4) are discussed. Complex 4 is active for the polymerization of acetylenes. Complex 4 polymerizes tert-butylacetylene to form cyclic poly(tert-butylacetylene). Evidence for a cyclic polymer topology comes from size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and intrinsic viscosity (η) measurements. This unusual reactivity of complex 4 toward a tert-alkylacetylene is attributed to its fluxional behavior, which arises from the double tethering of an yne-ol proligand (2) that facilitates monomer access and catalytic turnover. The preliminary scope of this complex design is demonstrated through modification of the yne-ol proligand, which afforded two additional double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complexes 10 and 11 that are also catalytically active for polymerization.

title: Electron-Catalyzed Supramolecular Assembly with High Efficiency, Robustness, and Versatility
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Although catalysis is widely exploited by nature to orchestrate noncovalent supramolecular assembly and build up complex living systems, its utilization in synthetic chemistry has conventionally been limited to accelerating covalent reactions. Consequently, the development of artificial systems for catalytic assembly remains a formidable and largely unexplored challenge. Here, we present a rationally designed strategy of electron-catalyzed supramolecular assembly, wherein the electron acts as an efficient, robust, and versatile catalyst to accelerate the formation of a donor–acceptor complex. Optimization of the elementary steps and intermediate stability yields an efficient catalytic cycle, furnishing the process with both a high turnover number and operational robustness in open air. Furthermore, the electron catalysis can be readily triggered by diverse external stimuli─including electricity, light, and mechanical force─enabling precise spatiotemporal control over the assembly process and near-quantitative synthesis of supramolecular complexes. Collectively, this work establishes a well-elucidated strategy of catalytic assembly with remarkable practicality, advancing the frontiers of noncovalent synthetic chemistry.

title: Role of (Co)substrate Coordination to Iron in Activating Its Two-Electron Reduction of Dioxygen: Mechanism of Pterin Activation in Tryptophan Hydroxylase
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Many O2-activating mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes require substrate or cofactor/cosubstrate coordination to iron to form the key peroxy-bridged intermediate necessary for catalysis with no net change in the iron redox state. The role of (co)substrate coordination, however, remained unclear. Here, we leverage a pterin-dependent enzyme, tryptophan hydroxylase, for which cosubstrate (pterin) coordination can be experimentally controlled by the absence and presence of substrate, to explicitly determine the role of pterin coordination in O2 binding and peroxo formation. EPR, absorption, circular dichroism, and magnetic circular dichroism spectroscopies on the {FeNO}7 analog of the unobservable {FeO2}8 intermediate without and with pterin coordination demonstrate that pterin coordination induces new absorption bands and enhances NO affinity by 3.6 kcal mol–1 at 277 K. These new bands are pterin-to-iron ligand-to-metal charge-transfer transitions that compensate the electron donation from iron to NO upon NO binding. Extension of our findings on {FeNO}7 to {FeO2}8 evidences that pterin coordination stabilizes O2 binding and facilitates the two-electron transfer from pterin to {FeO2}8 to reduce the transition-state barrier for peroxo formation by 12.7 kcal mol–1, corresponding to a 1010 increase in reaction rate. The electron transfer pathways established herein underscore a unified mechanism for the pterin-dependent, α-ketoglutarate-dependent, extradiol, and intradiol dioxygenase families of mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes through which (co)substrate coordination enhances O2 binding via one-electron transfer within {FeO2}8 and two-electron donation from the (co)substrate (one to bound O2 and one to iron) to generate the peroxo species with no net redox change on the iron.

title: A Crystalline LaCl3 Reinforced Amorphous Oxyhalide Electrolyte for Thermally Stable All-Solid-State Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are a promising next-generation energy storage technology, but their development is often constrained by the thermal instability and high cost of solid-state electrolytes (SSEs). Amorphous oxyhalide electrolytes, while mechanically deformable, are particularly susceptible to thermal degradation. Here, we report a novel and cost-effective composite SSE fabricated by embedding LaCl3 nanocrystals within an amorphous Li–Al–O–Cl (LAOC) matrix. This unique architecture synergistically combines the high ionic conductivity of the amorphous phase with the enhanced thermal and mechanical robustness imparted by the crystalline phase. The resulting Li–La–Al–O–Cl electrolyte achieves a high room-temperature ionic conductivity exceeding 1 mS cm–1 and demonstrates exceptional thermal stability, remaining a solid powder at 150 °C, a temperature at which the baseline LAOC melts. This enhanced thermal and thermo-mechanical integrity, combined with excellent deformability, enables superior interfacial contact and stability with cathodes. The Li–La–Al–O–Cl-based ASSBs maintain stable operation at 80 °C, in stark contrast to the rapid failure of LAOC-based cells. This strategy of reinforcing a soft amorphous matrix with a rigid crystalline offers a new pathway for designing thermally robust, high-performance, and commercially viable SSEs.

title: Molecular Mechanophores Based on Stress-Enhanced Exciton Transition between Phosphorescent Probes and Polymer Matrix
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Mechanophores provide an in situ and remote tool for quantifying invisible stress in polymers by photonic signals, offering distinct advantages for stress distribution analysis of large-area surfaces and instrument-free stress observation. However, achieving an ideal mechanophore that integrates with sensitive, reversible, and molecular-level stress sensing is attractive yet challenging. Here, we report practical guidance for developing ideal mechanophores that promote the molecular probe’s exciton transition for room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) under stress, through the “assisted lowest triplet (T1) state” of the adjacent polymer chain.
