title: Anti -Dihydroxylation-Enabled Dual-Resolution Profiling and Imaging of Fatty Acid C═C Bond Isomers
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Lipids are essential for membrane structure, signaling, and stress adaptation. Their diverse biological roles are largely dictated by the presence of C═C bonds in unsaturated fatty acids (FAs), which vary in both position and geometry. However, unambiguous characterization and in situ mapping of these two structural features have remained longstanding analytical challenges. Here, we present a stereochemistry-preserved chemical derivatization strategy coupled with trapped ion mobility spectrometry-tandem MS (TIMS-MS/MS), enabling complete resolution of both FA C═C bond position and geometry within a single workflow. This approach facilitates rapid and quantitative profiling of dynamic cis–trans isomerization in bacteria under diverse stress conditions and, notably, reveals a previously unrecognized dose-dependent antibiotic adaptation mechanism in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a multidrug-resistant pathogen. To translate this strategy to spatially resolved analyses, we developed an in situ derivatization workflow for mass spectrometry imaging, which uncovers the spatial heterogeneity of FA isomers in proximally cocultured, clinically relevant polymicrobial pathogens. These findings highlight colony-specific spatial dynamics of cis and trans lipid isomers and suggest lipid-mediated metabolic interactions between co-occurring microbial species. Together, this integrated platform enables both quantitative and spatial interrogation of lipid isomerization, providing new opportunities to systematically investigate its roles in microbial physiology, pathogenesis, and beyond.

title: Reprogramming ThDP-Dependent Enzyme for Intermolecular [3 + 2] Annulation via a Homoenolate Intermediate
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Thiamine diphosphate (ThDP)-dependent enzymes are versatile biocatalysts for carbon–carbon bond formation, yet their catalytic repertoire has been largely confined to linear homologation and intramolecular cyclizations that rely on single-site reactive intermediates such as the Breslow or ketyl radical species. Intermolecular annulation─a powerful strategy for constructing cyclic architectures─has remained elusive within this enzyme class. Here, we report the first intermolecular [3 + 2] annulation catalyzed by a ThDP-dependent enzyme, achieved through a homoenolate-mediated nucleophilic addition pathway. A phylogeny-guided enzyme mining identified a previously uncharacterized enzyme from Variovorax boronicumulans(ThDP-5), and subsequent protein engineering yielded the F484S variant, which exhibits markedly enhanced activity and exquisite stereocontrol. This biocatalytic system exhibits a broad substrate scope (30 examples), accommodating diverse substituted cinnamaldehydes and isatins to afford chiral spirooxindole lactones with excellent stereoselectivity (up to > 20:1 dr and 99% ee). Preparative-scale reactions (2 mmol) validate its synthetic utility. This work expands ThDP-dependent biocatalysis to intermolecular annulations, providing a robust and selective platform for the construction of pharmaceutically relevant spirocyclic architectures.

title: Interfacial Confinement Enables Conformal IrOx Nanofilms for Low-Ir-Loading PEM Water Electrolysis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Terawatt-scale deployment of proton-exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) requires low iridium (Ir) loading, which disrupts the catalyst layer’s in-plane electronic percolation network and severely degrades performance. Here, we overcome this bottleneck via an interfacial confinement strategy that electrostatically enriches cationic Ir intermediates on the negatively charged, oxygen-deficient TiOx surface, thereby redirecting Ir deposition from three-dimensional island growth to a two-dimensional conformal film on TiO2 supports. The resulting IrOx-NF@TiO2 catalyst with low Ir packing density maintains long-range in-plane electron percolation, reducing reliance on the high Ir loading typically required by conventional IrOx nanoparticle catalysts to establish quasi-continuous conductive pathways. At a loading of 0.166 mgIr cm−2, blade-coated membrane electrode assemblies incorporating this architecture feature ∼7 μm-thick catalyst layers with an Ir packing density of only ∼0.25 gIr cm–3, allowing an ∼84% reduction in Ir use while achieving performance comparable to that of commercial IrO2. This work highlights the potential of supported conformal IrOx catalysts as competitive candidates for next-generation low-Ir PEMWEs.

title: Solvent/Anion Codepleted Solvation Engineering Enables Low-Coordination Electrolytes for High-Energy and Low-Temperature Sodium-Ion Pouch Cells
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Widespread deployment of sodium-ion batteries demands both high energy density and reliable low-temperature (LT) operation, but is constrained by a persistent trade-off between high-voltage stability (cathode/electrolyte) and LT ion-transport kinetics. Herein, we report a solvent/anion codepleted solvation engineering strategy to construct low-coordination electrolytes through competitive anion complexation mediated by a bulky electron-deficient additive, TMSB (tris(trimethylsilyl)borate). We reveal that TMSB preferentially complexes with PF6– to suppress direct anion-Na+ coordination, while its bulky steric backbone disrupts conventional ion-pair networks and restricts excessive solvent-Na+ coordination. This strategy fundamentally boosts ionic conductivity (from 2.41 to 5.34 mS cm–1) and lowers the desolvation energy barrier (from 44.82 to 33.97 kJ mol–1). Moreover, such a strategy enables a high-modulus (2.7 GPa), inorganic-rich cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI), which can not only mitigate surface degradation, but also suppress bulk phase transitions of cathode materials. Consequently, the electrolyte demonstrates broad compatibility across diverse cathodes (NFM, NVP, and P2-NNMO) under extreme voltage (up to 4.5 V) and temperature (−40 to 25 °C) conditions. Remarkably, the scaled-up 6.8 Ah pouch cell achieves a record-high energy density of 200 Wh kg–1 at 25 °C, while maintaining 162 Wh kg–1 even at −20 °C, offering a generalizable molecular paradigm for extreme-environment energy storage.

title: A Single Water Molecule Drives a 20-Fold Acceleration in the Gas-Phase Reaction of Iodide with Ozone
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Iodine chemistry has an outsized role in the atmosphere and environment due to its highly reactive nature. Unlike chlorine and bromine, around 80% of atmospheric iodine is emitted directly from the ocean through the reaction of iodide and ozone at the sea surface. Uncertainties remain, however, in the effects of hydration, salinity, temperature, and other factors on this globally significant reaction. Using linear ion-trap mass spectrometry, a single water molecule is shown here to provide a 23 (±6)-fold acceleration to the rate of iodide oxidation. The first step in reaction of both I– and I–·H2O with ozone is oxidation to IO– with subsequent fast reactions to yield IO3–. No evidence is found for direct routes from I–·H2O to IO2– nor any incorporation of the water oxygen into ionic products. Ab initio calculations show that the initial rate-determining step for both reactions proceeds on the singlet surface with water playing an active role to lower the barrier through hydrogen bonding. Kinetic modeling based on the computed energetics is in excellent agreement with experimental measurements and enables extrapolation of this reaction to lower temperatures relevant to polar regions and the ozone layer. This analysis shows that (i) I– may outcompete I• for ozone destruction as temperature decreases, and (ii) I–·H2O reacts more than an order of magnitude faster than I• over 350 to 230 K. This work demonstrates that iodide has a previously underappreciated role in multiphase ozone destruction in the atmosphere and lays the foundation for understanding microscopic environmental influences in salt clusters and nanodroplets.

title: Trends in nitrogen management across European agricultural systems reveal progress since 1980s and required considerable improvements
abstract: Abstract Nitrogen (N) inefficiency threatens both environmental sustainability and food production in European agriculture, with many regions facing high levels of N pollution. Addressing the dual challenge of sustaining productivity while reducing environmental harm requires an integrated, spatially explicit indicator. We present the Environmental Nitrogen Management Index (ENMI) — a threshold-based, composite indicator that captures agricultural productivity (N yield relative to regional target yield) and environmental pressure (N surplus relative to regional safe N surplus). ENMI ranges from 0 (worst) to 1 (sustainable: no adverse impacts at target yield). Applied across EU sub-national regions from the 1960s to 2010s, ENMI rose from 0.07 to 0.21, with disparities from 0.76 in Switzerland to below 0.1 in parts of Eastern Europe. A 2030 scenario analysis shows that ambitious N input cuts improve environmental outcomes but reduce yields. ENMI offers a transparent basis to assess sustainability progress and guide policy interventions on N management.

title: Mechanocatalysis: From energy coupling to electronic behavior
abstract: Mechanocatalysis harnesses ubiquitous mechanical energy for sustainable chemical transformations, but its development is hindered by conceptual fragmentation. This review proposes a process-oriented framework, deconstructing mechanocatalysis into four sequential stages: energy coupling, transduction, charge transport, and electronic behavior. This framework provides a mechanistic basis for the rational design of mechanocatalytic systems, paving the way for standardized evaluation and broader applications.

title: Mapping the Slow Propagation of Disorder across a Photoreceptor’s Tertiary Structure with Time-Resolved Crystallography
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Order–disorder transitions allow many proteins to shift between compact and flexible/unfolded states, thereby acting as structural switches that regulate catalysis, signaling, recognition, and allostery. We applied time-resolved serial oscillation crystallography to establish the structural kinetics of the light-triggered order–disorder transition of an animal-like cryptochrome as a six-second-long molecular movie with near-atomic all-residue spatial resolution and millisecond temporal resolution. Our 29 structural snapshots mapped the propagation of disorder across the tertiary structure motifs of a cryptochrome’s C-terminal region, triggered by a single broken D321–R492 salt bridge. The order–disorder transition followed a nucleation-propagation mechanism reminiscent of helix–coil dynamics and proceeded over up to five seconds, with regions distal to the D321–R492 trigger initially undergoing slow zero-order disordering before switching to first-order unfolding kinetics. Our per-residue density analysis provides a detailed structural-kinetic basis for understanding how order–disorder transitions emerge through directional propagation across protein tertiary structures, as occurring in signaling and many other biological systems.

title: Low-Temperature-Mediated Lamellar–Micelle Assembly of Wrinkled Mesoporous Carbon Nanospheres with Aligned Pores and High Interconnectivity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Mesoporous structures with highly permeable channels are of great significance for fast diffusion; however, the delicate engineering of straightforward pores remains quite limited, with most of mesostructures are tortuous pores derived from spherical micelle assembly. Herein, we explore a novel lamellar–micelle assembly approach that enables to generate a type of wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres with highly interconnected divergent mesopores. In place of the conventional spherical micelles, the key for controlling such unusual assembly is determined by the construction of laminar micelles (copolymer L121/F127 composite) and heterogeneous growth on sedimented F127 seeds at a low temperature of 5 °C. The fabricated wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres after template removal possess a particle size at ∼910 nm, a high surface area of 315 m2 g–1, a uniform pore size at 36 nm, as well as radial mesochannels with high interconnectivity up to 96%. Further regulation on the reaction temperature and template ratio allows for a high tunability over the pore size and wrinkle degree. When employed as a sodium storage anode, the radially aligned large-pore structure drastically facilitates charge transport and electrolyte penetration, thus delivering rate capability (142 mAh g–1 at 10 A g–1) and long-term cyclability (90.5% retention after 1000 cycles at 2 A g–1) compared to commercial hard carbon. Our work underscores a particular assembly pathway through lamellar micelles as an effective approach for building up ultrafast mesopore highways toward promising diffusion-related applications.

title: Control of Charge Carrier Dynamics and Bandgap Renormalization in CdS Quantum Dot Hybrids by Interface Polarity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Charge carrier dynamics in wurtzite CdS quantum dots (QDs) form the basis for applications in optoelectronics and photocatalysis. We demonstrate that the quantum dynamics, energy gaps, and energy level alignments at CdS QD interfaces can be controlled by the polarity of the CdS QD surface. By performing nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations within a density-functional tight-binding framework, we demonstrate a strong dependence of photoinitiated processes in CdS QDs/graphene nanoribbon (GNR) hybrids on interface polarity. At room temperature, hole transfer is accelerated by a factor of 2 and exciton lifetime is enhanced by nearly an order of magnitude when the CdS QD surface is switched from polar to nonpolar. Remarkably, the interfacial bandgap for the polar QD/GNR hybrid is reduced to half upon heating from 0 K to room temperature, while it remains nearly unchanged for the nonpolar hybrid. At an intermediate temperature, the ultrafast charge separation is maintained; however, charge recombination shows the opposite trend relative to room temperature. The polar interface exhibits a longer lifetime than the nonpolar interface, due to weakened electron–phonon Fröhlich interaction and decreased gap renormalization. The strong and highly nonlinear dependence of bandgap renormalization and carrier dynamics on temperature in the polar QD/GNR hybrid is associated with significant structural reconstruction, which is absent in the nonpolar counterpart. The demonstrated control of excited-state processes by interface polarity and the strong dependence of the dynamics and energy level alignment on temperature provide key fundamental insights for informed design of modern materials for optoelectronics and energy conversion.

title: Simultaneous Selective Recognition of Two Different Anions within a Hydrogen/Halogen-Bonding Cage
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The search for selective anion receptors that can function in water is a longstanding challenge in supramolecular chemistry, motivated by anions’ fundamental roles (and potential applications) in biological, environmental, and industrial processes. Here, we incorporate halogen and hydrogen bond donors into an easy-to-prepare organic cage molecule and demonstrate that this can bind anions at either or both of a halogen-bonding pocket and hydrogen-bonding pockets depending on the nature of the anions and the solvent. The halogen-bonding pocket comprising six bromopyridinium donors is a potent host for iodide anions and can selectively bind this guest in water as strongly as biological iodide binders (Ka = 43,000 M–1 measured by 1H NMR spectroscopy) with the exclusion of other halide anions. In DMSO/water mixtures, the hydrogen-bonding pockets are able to recognize chloride anions, resulting in the formation of mixed anion iodide/chloride complexes with an iodide bound in the center of the cage and chlorides in the peripheral binding sites. This demonstrates the exquisite selectivity afforded by halogen-bonding systems and reveals a general route to a range of supramolecular anion hosts that bind multiple guests in different locations.

title: Limited genomic predictability of complex trait evolution despite genotype-phenotype stability
abstract: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown. Here, we tested the efficacy of genomic prediction of complex trait evolution by monitoring genome-wide allele frequencies and pigmentation variation in genetically diverse populations of Drosophila melanogaster during evolution in both field mesocosms and a controlled, lab-based setting. At two points during trait evolution, we produced a high-powered, well-resolved genotype-phenotype map that exhibited marked stability across independent populations. Although we were able to use this map to correctly infer the direction of pigmentation evolution in both the lab and field settings, the particular loci responding to selection were largely unpredictable based on the direction of trait evolution itself. Our results hold implications for the promise, and limitations, of genomic prediction.

title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

title: Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants
abstract: Humans and many other animals live in interconnected social communities that are essential for survival and well-being. In principle, communities can persist despite changes in constituent members. However, gradually accumulating changes to membership could push systems past critical thresholds into alternate states, restructuring patterns of connectivity. Such changes can further affect systemic resilience against disturbance. We investigated social network dynamics for 443 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years by tracking community membership and structure. Following accumulated demographic turnover, networks fractured into smaller and more isolated communities. Connections changed not only owing to loss of members but also modifications in relationships among remaining individuals. This provides empirical evidence of a persistent state change in the social network of a long-lived terrestrial mammal following gradually accumulating demographic turnover.

title: Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around β Pictoris
abstract: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. We infer that the CO 2 ice is intimately mixed with the water ice at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April–May 2026
abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.

title: The genetic landscape of canine tumors: Insights from the Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA)
abstract: The Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA, https://caninecancergenomeatlas.org/ ) is an open, accessible comparative oncology resource that harmonizes whole-exome data across 10 canine tumor histotypes. It aggregates 667 tumor-normal pairs with curated single-nucleotide variants, insertions and deletions, structural variants, and copy number aberrations. Cohort-depth stratification distinguished primary, exploratory, and descriptive analyses. Selection analyses identified 39 cancer drivers, including recurrent TP53 , PIK3CA , PTEN , SETD2 , MAP3K14 , and FAT4 alterations; copy number events included MYC amplifications and PTEN deletions. Direct comparison with matched human cancers revealed conserved and species-enriched oncogenic mechanisms, pathways, and therapeutic contexts. The CCGA standardizes alignment, variant calling, and annotation through consensus pipelines and provides downloadable data and interactive analyses. This reusable framework advances precision veterinary oncology and strengthens translational bridges to human cancer, supporting comparative and translational research.

title: TMEM184 proteins are Ca 2+ uptake transporters in lysosomes
abstract: Lysosomal Ca 2+ release from acidic stores is critical for lysosomal function, yet the molecular identity of the Ca 2+ uptake conduit has remained elusive. We used a Ca 2+ -imaging–based genetic screen of the lysosomal membrane proteome to identify TMEM184 family proteins as lysosomal Ca 2+ transporters (LyCaTs) essential for Ca 2+ uptake and refilling. TMEM184 selectively transported Ca 2+ while excluding monovalent cations. Loss of TMEM184B/C depleted lysosomal Ca 2+ stores, diminished Ca 2+ release, and disrupted lysosomal exocytosis, biogenesis, and membrane repair, thus phenocopying the release channel transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1) deficiency. Moreover, a human TMEM184B mutation associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder compromised lysosomal Ca 2+ transport, and Tmem184b -deficient mice exhibited profound motor impairment. Thus, TMEM184 constitutes the long-sought Ca 2+ uptake and refilling mechanism that governs lysosomal signaling and homeostasis.

title: Quantitative measurement of viscosity in two-dimensional electron fluids
abstract: Electron hydrodynamics is an emerging framework that describes dynamics of interacting electron systems as conventional fluids. Although evidence for hydrodynamic-like transport has been reported in a variety of two-dimensional materials, precise quantitative measurement of the core parameter, electron viscosity, remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate that magnetoresistance in Corbino-shaped graphene devices offers a simultaneous ohmmeter and viscosometer capability, allowing us to disentangle the individual ohmic and viscous contributions to transport, even near viscous-ohmic crossover. In both monolayer and bilayer graphene, the effective electron-electron scattering rate scales linearly with temperature, deviating markedly from the T 2 dependence expected in conventional Fermi liquids. Instead, it is consistent with a recently identified tomographic fluid regime, theoretically predicted to be generic for two-dimensional electron systems.

title: A trapped catalytic product acts as molecular glue for innate immune signalosome assembly
abstract: Innate immune systems of living organisms are essential for host defense. Central to these systems is the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain, an evolutionarily conserved module. From antiphage systems in prokaryotes to innate immune systems in plants, TIR domains have catalytic activity. However, TIR domains within animal innate immune receptors, such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), have been considered as scaffolds for adaptor recruitment. We report that the TLR4 TIR domain possesses an allosterically activated nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) hydrolase (NADase) activity that operates in a single-turnover manner. Its product, adenosine diphosphate ribose, is not released but entrapped as a “molecular glue,” stabilizing a composite catalytic pocket with adaptor TIR domain–containing adaptor protein (TIRAP) to nucleate signalosome assembly. This “produce-and-trap” mechanism represents a signaling mode that integrates enzymatic activity with adaptor function to drive downstream signaling.

title: Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore
abstract: After the African origin of Homo sapiens , multiple dispersals radiated into Asia, yet the Saharo-Arabian archaeological record remains sparse. In this study, we report on ‘Uruq Aljelibah, a Middle Paleolithic site dated to ~125,000 years ago (marine isotope stage 5e) and located on the shore of Mundafan paleolake, Saudi Arabia. Levallois assemblages, refits, and megafaunal associations indicate in situ tool production and carcass processing. Stone tool residues, use-wear, and biomarkers reveal animal and plant processing, including palms, tubers, trees, and shrubs. Several points exhibit impact damage and poison residues (from Acokanthera schimperi ), indicating use as hafted weapon tips within composite hunting systems. Megafaunal remains include hippopotamus, buffalo, gazelle, ostrich, and camel, illuminating hominin use of freshwater and grassland ecosystems.

title: Climate aridity amplifies global riverine nitrate beyond human inputs
abstract: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Here we show, with machine-learning reconstructed global maps, that climate aridity is also a dominant driver, systematically elevating nitrate concentrations across land-use gradients and creating unexpected hotspots beyond major agricultural and urban centers. Across ~2.9 million river segments worldwide, nitrate concentrations exceed ecological and health thresholds across ~33 and 2% of global land area, affecting ~5.6 billion (73%) and 0.5 billion (6%) people, respectively. Ecological threshold exceedance occurs mostly in headwaters, and about half of the health threshold exceedance occurs in middle-income countries and sparsely populated landscapes. These findings cast nitrate pollution as an aridity-amplified risk, suggesting that aridification may increase nitrate exposure even without additional human inputs. They call for regulatory standards that reflect risks across broad concentration ranges.

title: Atmospheric O 2 reveals a strengthening ocean carbon sink and a stagnant net land sink since 1990
abstract: The global ocean and land biosphere absorb roughly half of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The temporal evolution of these sinks remains difficult to quantify owing to data sparsity. Leveraging 30+ years of atmospheric oxygen (O 2 ) and CO 2 observations, we find that the ocean carbon sink increased by 0.63 ± 0.19 petagrams of carbon per year per decade (Pg C year −1 decade −1 ) (a mean of 2.8 ± 0.4 Pg C year −1 ), accounting for 35% of fossil emissions between 1990 and 2019. The net land sink shows no robust trend (with a mean of 1.0 ± 0.5 Pg C year −1 , accounting for 13% of fossil emissions), despite large decadal variability. These results challenge many process-based model simulations of the land and ocean sinks, questioning their ability to accurately predict future climate states.

title: ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering drive extracellular vesicle budding from cilia
abstract: Cilia-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate cell-cell communication and remove signaling molecules from cilia. The Hedgehog receptor Smoothened (SMO) is selected for packaging into ciliary EVs by ubiquitin chains, but how cargo selection is coupled to EV budding remains unknown. In this work, working in mouse kidney cells, we found that the ubiquitin reader endosomal sorting complex required for transport–0 (ESCRT-0) orchestrates both cargo selection and EV biogenesis. Unlike the conventional ESCRT pathway, SMO secretion did not require the ESCRT-III membrane scission machinery. Instead, ESCRT-0 condensed at the ciliary tip, where it clustered ubiquitinated SMO to drive EV biogenesis. Disrupting ESCRT-0 condensation blocked SMO secretion, and combining forced recruitment of ESCRT-0 with optogenetic clustering of SMO was sufficient to reconstitute EV budding. Thus, ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering constitute a minimal module for ESCRT-III–independent reverse-topology budding.

title: Geodetic observations in West Antarctica reveal geodynamically consistent 3D mantle viscosity
abstract: The rapid ice loss in West Antarctica since the 1990s has led to substantial ice surface lowering, regional bedrock uplift, and gravity reduction, as measured by geodetic observations. The bedrock (crustal) motions and gravity changes result from glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), a process controlled by Earth’s viscoelastic properties and deglaciation history. In this study, we present GIA models with geodynamically consistent three-dimensional mantle viscoelastic structures and reconstructed ice history for Antarctica from 1900 to 2020, which explain both the observed Global Navigation Satellite System crustal motions and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment gravity changes in West Antarctica. This study demonstrates that a mantle rheology including a weak asthenosphere and temperature-dependent viscosity is consistent with both mantle convection at million-year timescales and ongoing decadal GIA occurring in West Antarctica.

title: Early epidemiological and spatial assessment of the Bundibugyo virus outbreak 2026
abstract: A Bundibugyo virus outbreak was first reported on May 15th, 2026 in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with multiple cases reported across health zones during the early phase of the outbreak and suggestions of circulation weeks prior to detection. We pair highly resolved case and testing records with human mobility data to investigate the early outbreak dynamics of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). We show that human movement was a principle driver of early spatial expansion between May 10th and June 1st when the number of health zones and health areas reporting positive cases increased by 12 and 49, respectively. The early doubling time was estimated at ~10 days. Our work shows the rapid spatial expansion and growth of BVD with implications for intervention strategies.

title: D-A-D Engineered Electrochromic Coordination Metallopolymers for Smart Windows, Energy Storage, and Wearables
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Electrochromic coordination metallopolymers featuring multi-redox centers and structural versatility offer great potential for smart windows and glazing, yet they are hampered in practical application owing to the intrinsic trade-off between optical modulation and charge storage. Herein, we introduce a benzothiadiazole acceptor to construct a donor–acceptor–donor architecture that enhances intramolecular charge transfer and enables intervalence charge transfer, narrowing the bandgap and improving near-infrared electrochromism and capacitance. The resulting BT-CMP//V2O5 device exhibits large optical contrast (ΔT > 50%), fast switching (1.7/3.8 s), and high coloration efficiency (>300 cm2·C–1), enabling efficient photothermal modulation with an annual energy saving of 155.19 MJ·m–2. The D-A-D architecture facilitates rapid and complete charge separation, endowing the polymer with superior energy storage performance, including a high areal capacitance of 38.24 mF·cm–2. Furthermore, flexible prototypes exhibit EC and energy storage, maintain stable performance after 100 bending cycles. This D-A-D strategy provides a versatile platform to overcome the intrinsic trade-off of electrochromic materials, paving the way for high-performance electrochromic energy storage devices.

title: Boosting Photocatalytic Performance via Electron Transfer Regulation in Biocomponent Hybrid Heterojunctions
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Against the backdrop of global climate change and the energy crisis, developing efficient and sustainable catalytic technologies is crucial for addressing environmental and energy challenges. Compared to traditional heterojunctions, the incorporation of natural biogenic components holds great potential for overcoming bottlenecks such as complex crystal engineering, insufficient stability, and limited selectivity. This review established an electron transfer regulation framework to guide the construction of biocomponent hybrid heterojunctions for superior photocatalysis. We systematically cover various biogenic components and their derivatives, from small molecules, conjugated polymers, and supramolecular assemblies, to three-dimensional networks and crystal frameworks such as metal–organic frameworks and covalent-organic frameworks. Based on in-depth mechanistic analysis, this review demonstrates how these biogenic components modulate band engineering, charge transfer kinetics, substrate utilization, and defect passivation, which collectively achieve sequential optimization across the entire charge-carrier lifecycle—from generation and transport to surface reaction and long-term stability. Importantly, all of these directly linked to enhanced photocatalytic performance in H2 evolution, CO2 reduction, H2O2 generation, and pollutant degradation. In addition to conventional band engineering, novel mechanisms such as exciton behavior modulation and conjugated continuity regulation are discussed. This framework transforms empirical material design into predictable catalysis optimization, aiming to accelerate the development of high-performance biocomponent hybrid heterojunctions.

title: Interfacial Solvent Engineering Enables Hydrothermally Stable MXene Heterostructures for Printed Wearable Electronics
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Water-induced degradation of MXene during hydrothermal synthesis severely limits the construction of MXene-based heterostructures for further applications. Herein, an interfacial solvent-engineering strategy was developed to stabilize MXene under harsh hydrothermal conditions. Solvents with a stronger affinity for reactive Ti sites than water can preferentially adsorb at these sites. This competitive adsorption limits direct water–Ti contact and thereby suppresses subsequent MXene oxidation. DFT calculations were used to screen candidate solvents and support the proposed competitive adsorption mechanism, while the experimental results broadly followed the predicted trend. Deoxygenation experiments further supported the dominant role of water in MXene degradation. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that preferential interfacial enrichment of DMF persists at 453 K despite enhanced thermal motion. In a 50 vol % DMF/H2O system, the MXene framework remained well preserved even under prolonged or higher-temperature hydrothermal treatment. This regulated solvent environment enabled the in situ growth of 1T-MoS2 on the preserved MXene framework. The conductive MXene framework and abundant active sites of 1T-MoS2 led to enhanced electrochemical performance. The resulting composite was further processed into printed microsupercapacitors and pressure sensors, which were integrated into a self-powered pressure-sensing system. This work establishes interfacial solvent engineering as an effective route to hydrothermally stable MXene heterostructures for printed wearable electronics.

title: Potential-Dependent Hydricities and Bond Dissociation Free Energies of Metal Surface Hydrides
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Recent experimental studies demonstrate that the thermodynamic hydricity of surface-bound intermediates is continuously tunable via electrical polarization. Canonical density functional theory relies on constant-charge models that fail to capture this potential-dependent polarization at the electrified solid-liquid interface. This work implements grand-canonical density functional theory (GC-DFT) to compute the surface hydricity, bond dissociation free energy (BDFE), and acidity of chemisorbed hydrogen across transition metal facets. Assuming an outer-sphere transfer isolates the intrinsic hydrogen-donating capacity of the active site. By explicitly controlling the system Fermi level, we demonstrate that surface hydricity exhibits a universal linear dependence on applied cathodic bias across all evaluated facets. In contrast, the potential dependence of the homolytic BDFE is strictly governed by material identity: platinum maintains a relatively static bond strength, while silver and copper exhibit potential-induced bond stabilization. The computed hydricity slopes for Pt facets quantitatively reproduce the experimentally measured polarization-dependent hydride-transfer sensitivity. Coordination geometry dictates the baseline donor capacity, with lower coordination atop sites on Ag and Cu functioning as significantly stronger hydride donors. Adlayer saturation perturbs the thermodynamic values in a metal-dependent manner, weakening hydride donation on silver but strengthening it on copper. However, at the two coverages examined, it does not substantially alter the voltage sensitivity of the thermodynamic properties. Evaluating voltage-dependent hydricity provides a thermodynamic framework for characterizing the intrinsic hydride- or hydrogen-donating ability of electrified solid-liquid interfaces.

title: SIP-enabled multi-omics reveals soil microbiome responses to drought and rehydration
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Soil microbial activity, and the balance of anabolic (carbon assimilating) and catabolic (CO2-releasing) processes, control the magnitude and direction of soil carbon fluxes. Soil hydration controls this activity, and with hydroclimate volatility increasing across many regions, microbial responses to drought-rewetting cycles urgently require quantification. We conducted rainfall exclusion experiments at two Mediterranean-type field sites, coupling isotope labeling with multi-omics, to link microbial growth, greenhouse gas fluxes, and the carbon sources driving both. Rehydration shortened apparent cell generation times from years to days within minutes. High-intensity drought lengthened the lag before growth resumed, yet metagenomic inference indicated post-drought enrichment of rapid-growth phenotypes. Drought and rehydration shifted the soil metabolome, implicating specific osmolytes in the microbial response and suggesting metabolite diversity modulates microbial function. These results constrain soil microbial activity rates and mechanisms underlying drought-rewetting responses and motivate further study of carbon cycling under increasingly volatile hydroclimates.

title: Extinction risks in deep-sea populations revealed by genomic data and ecological niche modeling
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: As the global biodiversity crisis accelerates across terrestrial and shallow marine systems, the extent of this collapse remains unknown within the deep sea. Despite encompassing most of the ocean, deep-sea ecosystems remain the planet’s final frontier. Within this vast realm, the mesopelagic zone represents a critical yet poorly understood habitat, particularly in terms of its conservation status. Here, we integrate genomic data with ecological niche modeling to assess and forecast the conservation status of five mesopelagic species in the Gulf of Mexico. Samples were collected from 2011 to 2023, representing one of the longest time-series datasets for mesopelagic fauna in oceanographic history. All species exhibit current effective population sizes below the minimum thresholds for long-term viability. Genomic diversity declined over a decade in some species at rates comparable to or exceeding those reported for threatened and endangered species. Demographic modeling indicates historical population declines across all species. Ecological niche models predict declining Gulf habitat suitability for most species under future climate change scenarios. Together, our results identify indicators associated with elevated extinction risk in Gulf mesopelagic species and raise the possibility of a broader, unnoticed crisis, challenging assumptions of stability and resilience in mesopelagic ecosystems.

title: Proximal redox coupling enables oxidation damping for stable water electrolysis
abstract: The design of atomically precise catalysts requires strategies that regulate their electronic and structural dynamics under operating conditions. While conventional doping can effectively tune bulk materials, it translates poorly to single-atom catalysts (SACs), in which isolated atoms lack extended coordination and are prone to oxidative instability. Here we design atomically dispersed Ru-O-Cr motifs that enable oxidation damping during acidic oxygen evolution. In situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy shows attenuated Ru oxidation synchronized with anticorrelated and partially reversible Cr redox evolution, consistent with proximity-dependent redox coupling. This buffered redox response is accompanied by bounded and partially reversible changes in the local metal-oxygen coordination environment. These coupled dynamics support proximity-coupled Ru-O-Cr redox units, enabling a 55.7-fold increased resistance against oxidation-induced Ru dissolution compared with conventional SACs. In proton exchange membrane water electrolysis, catalysts incorporating proximal Ru-O-Cr configurations exhibit degradation rates that are 6.8-fold and 14.4-fold lower than those of Ru SACs and commercial RuO2, respectively, at 1 A cm-2. These results suggest proximal oxidation damping as a potential design principle for stabilizing atomically precise electrocatalysts.

title: Covalent sulfur-rich a-CoS5 as a sulfur-equivalent cathode material for Li-S batteries with larger gravimetric and volumetric capacities
abstract: Different from the problematic elemental sulfur cathodes that suffer from severe polysulfide shuttling, the prepared a-CoS5 stabilizes an unprecedentedly high covalent sulfur content (∼73 wt %) and enables highly reversible S–S bond cleavage and reformation without forming dissolved polysulfides. As a result, it delivers an exceptionally large capacity and long cyclability, thus establishing new benchmarks for simultaneously achieving high sulfur content and long cyclability among currently reported sulfur and sulfur-equivalent cathode materials for Li-S batteries.

ISG15 promotes PARP inhibitor resistance in BRCA1-deficient cells by facilitating DNA replication and repair
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The use of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) has proven largely successful in targeting BRCA1/2-mutated tumours. However, the emergence of PARPi-resistant disease can reduce the efficacy of this treatment, posing significant challenges in the clinic. Here, we use multiple models of BRCA1-/- cells and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) that have been treated with PARPi until they no longer responded to the drug, to characterise genomic and transcriptomic alterations specific to PARPi resistance. We find that abrogation of TP53BP1 expression occurs spontaneously during prolonged PARPi treatment, alongside TP53BP1 genomic deletions and promoter methylation. Additionally, innate immune response genes, including ISG15 and factors of the ISGylation machinery are upregulated in PARPi-resistant cells and tumours. We demonstrate that ISG15 inhibition re-sensitises PARPi-resistant cells to the drug and, conversely, that ISG15 overexpression in BRCA1-/- cells promotes PARPi resistance. Mechanistically, BRCA1-/- PARPi-resistant cells rely on ISG15 for replication fork progression and restart of stalled forks and for DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair via homologous recombination (HR). Our results indicate that complex ISG15 interactions with DNA replication/repair factors can drive PARPi resistance in BRCA1-deficient cancer cells and that targeting ISG15 has the potential to overcome PARPi resistance.

title: Structural basis of ligand-mediated transition to higher-order rubisco assemblies
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Proteins often assemble as higher order complexes, underlying a diversity of molecular structures and biological functions. The emergence of protein-protein interactions between binding partners is generally considered to be the primary driver of oligomerization. However, ligand binding has also been demonstrated to affect higher-order assembly, though this phenomenon is not widely considered as a primary driver of oligomerization. Here, we describe the mechanism by which different rubisco oligomeric states are induced via ligand binding. By expanding the phylogenetic sampling of a unique clade of rubisco, we discover a range of oligomeric responses to ligand binding across the phylogeny and identify the structural features responsible for shifts in the oligomeric state that ultimately provide a path to evolving new quaternary structures. Here, we identify a ligand-dependent mechanism giving rise to new protein assemblies, in contrast with the typical process of evolving new protein-protein interfaces directly. Our findings describe a means by which binding and entrenchment of a ligand enables an increase in structural complexity.

title: Turning inward: Constructing an expanded azahelicene cavity
Evolution of the molybdenum and vanadium cycles through time and their impact on ancient nitrogen fixation
source: Earth and environmental sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Biological nitrogen (N2) fixation is crucial for incorporating atmospheric N2 into the biosphere. However, its evolutionary trajectory remains enigmatic, particularly given the presumed scarcity of molybdenum (Mo) in Archean seawater prior to oxidative weathering and the apparent early emergence of Mo-based nitrogenase over its vanadium (V)-based alternatives. Here, we integrate partitioning experiments with an extensive analysis of iron-rich sediments through time to investigate the behavior of Mo and V in ancient seawater. Our results suggest that, during the Archean to Paleoproterozoic, dissolved V was removed from seawater more efficiently than Mo, primarily through preferential incorporation into banded iron formations (BIF). Consequently, Mo was likely more available in seawater than commonly assumed, with Archean seawater characterized by higher Mo/V ratios than today. Greater Mo availability relative to V provides a compelling explanation for the earlier evolution of Mo-based nitrogenase despite the absence of widespread oxidative weathering, and helps resolve the apparent paradox surrounding the early evolution of biological N2 fixation.

title: Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework and the Hybrid-Maize model (1991–2024) across five U.S. Corn Belt states, we quantify climate-driven yield contributions and show that they transition from southern declines to northern gains, reflecting the persistent influence of the central U.S. summer warming hole characterized by cooling maximum temperatures and increasing rainfall. A systematic thermal mismatch between environmental heat availability and hybrid growing degree day requirements is observed, particularly south of 42°N, where thermal matching declined despite favorable thermal conditions. Contrasting trends in thermal matching and reproductive duration help explain the latitude-dependent structure of climate-driven yield contributions. Our findings highlight how hybrid selection modulates the impacts of temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and radiation trends on maize yield gains across the U.S. Corn Belt.

title: Quantitative Solvation Scale for Lithium Battery Electrolytes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Understanding electrolyte solvation is vital for developing advanced lithium batteries, as solvation structures dictate interfacial chemistry and performance. This study evaluates the reliability of conventional 1D NMR techniques (1H, 7Li, 19F, and 13C) for probing lithium solvation. We demonstrate that absolute chemical shifts often correlate poorly with solvating ability, leading to misleading interpretations—a finding cross-validated by FTIR and DOSY. We identify that the change in chemical shift (Δδ) from 13C NMR serves as a robust descriptor, provided that the probe solvent’s solvating ability matches the system. To overcome single-probe limitations, we introduce a multiprobe strategy using ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), trifluoroethyl methyl carbonate (FEMC), and propylene carbonate (PC). This approach establishes a quantitative solvation scale across weak, intermediate, and strong solvating regimes. The resulting scale shows strong linear correlations with coordination ratios and solvating power, enabling precise linear free-energy relationships. We demonstrate the practical utility of this framework by accurately predicting lithium nitrate solubility and guiding electrolyte design. Ultimately, this work provides a reliable, broadly applicable methodology for advancing next-generation battery electrolytes. Most importantly, this work provides a lithium solvating strength series, offering a highly useful tool for researchers to compare common solvents.

title: Constructing exclusive Pt@WOx interfacial sites enables selective C–O bond activation
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Precisely constructing exclusive metal-oxide interfacial active sites while eliminating non-interfacial species represents a longstanding challenge in heterogeneous catalysis. Here we construct catalysts featuring exclusively isolated Pt@WOx interfacial sites via a controlled electrostatic adsorption strategy, thereby eliminating non-interfacial Pt species, enabling controlled reaction pathways. We identify that selective C–O bond activation is governed by the availability of interfacial reactive hydrogen, where isolated Pt sites drive deep hydrogenolysis, while Pt@WOx interfacial sites control reaction pathways by constrained hydrogen availability. This principle is validated in glycerol hydrogenolysis, achieving a high 1,3-PDO selectivity of 73.5% at a low temperature of 130 °C. Experiments reveal that 1,3-PDO selectivity is not enhanced by increasing active site density, but by eliminating intrinsically unselective sites, thereby reshaping the reaction energy landscape to suppress thermodynamically driven over-hydrogenolysis. This architecture provides an ideal platform for disentangling interface effects from contributions arising from non-interfacial metal species.

title: Cobalt based anode for highly stable alkaline water electrolysis under operation conditions beyond industrial requirements
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Alkaline water electrolysis is the most established route to electrochemical hydrogen production, but the limited lifetime of anode catalysts makes long-term equipment investment costly and hinders miniaturization. Here we show that, unlike the extensively investigated nickel- and nickel–iron-based hydroxides, the long-neglected cobalt–nickel hydroxides are promising anode catalysts whose stability exceeds current industrial requirements. A cobalt–nickel layered double hydroxide anode enables stable alkaline water electrolysis for more than 8,000 hours at 1 A cm–2 in 6 M sodium hydroxide at 80 °C. This stability arises from the strengthened metal–oxygen bonding of the in-situ-formed cobalt–nickel oxyhydroxide, which raises the energy barrier for lattice-oxygen loss during the oxygen evolution reaction. In a practical electrolyzer, the anode achieves an energy consumption of ~4.2 kWh per normal cubic metre of hydrogen at 1 A cm–2 and operates stably for thousands of hours. The design of high-current-density alkaline electrolyzers should therefore prioritize robust anode stability under industrial conditions in addition to activity optimization.

title: Emergent stoichiometric host-guest recognition on ligated colloidal surfaces via dynamic ligand reorientation
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Physical adsorption on ligand-protected colloidal nanoparticles is central to their properties and applications, yet adsorption events on dynamic ligand shells are rarely defined, counted, or quantified with molecular precision. Here we show that on a native ligand shell without pre-designed receptor-like motifs, molecular adsorption can trigger stoichiometric host-guest recognition through dynamic ligand reorientation. In aqueous dispersion, atomically precise [Au25(p-MBA)18]− (p-MBA = para-mercaptobenzoic acid) nanoclusters accommodate tetraalkylammonium ions within transient aromatic pockets formed by three to four neighboring p-MBA ligands. NMR titration and diffusion-ordered spectroscopy reveal an apparent saturated binding number of six guests per nanocluster, with an apparent association constant of ~3.5 × 104 M−1 and ΔG of ~−25 kJ•mol−1 for tetrapropylammonium binding. Molecular simulations and free-energy analysis rationalize this stoichiometry through a cooperative yet self-limiting mechanism, in which ligand reorientation creates bowl-like pockets stabilized by multiple CH···π interactions while steric constraints limit further guest accommodation. The guest-size- and surface-dependent binding behaviors further reveal the adaptive nature of emergent pockets. These findings change the role of the ligand shell from a stabilizing layer or diffuse adsorption medium to an active supramolecular interface capable of producing molecularly defined recognition, paving the way for adaptive nanomaterials, selective sensing, and stimuli-responsive colloidal systems.

title: Six-dimensional programmable ultrasonic vibration for multimodal object manipulation
abstract: Object manipulation via external stimuli is a pivotal technology across physics, engineering, and materials science. However, the strict material requirements and complex manipulation systems of existing approaches limit the operational flexibility, functional versatility, and material adaptability. Here we present an approach for generating six-dimensional (6D) programmable ultrasonic vibration. The 6D vibration consists of three-dimensional (3D) translational vibration and 3D rotational vibration, generated through coupling and superposing of multiple longitudinal and bending vibration modes. Selective spatiotemporal combination of these vibration components enables the construction of programmable vibration fields. Most importantly, we realize multimodal manipulation of individual and collective objects positioned on a 6D vibrating surface, including trapping, translation, rotation, bounce, and reconfiguration. We demonstrate highly adaptive manipulation of objects with various shapes, materials, and scales. Furthermore, diverse applications are conducted at both the macroscale and microscale. This work opens avenues for the development of ultrasound manipulation.

title: Autapse-inspired neuromorphic hardware with synapse–neuron integration for bidirectional feedback control
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Establishing autonomous and energy-efficient feedback control at the hardware level remains challenging because conventional systems rely on centralized processing and continuous external computation, increasing energy consumption and system complexity. Here we show a neuromorphic autapse-inspired system that enables localized and bidirectional feedback control, using thermoregulation as a representative application. An autapse is a self-synaptic connection in which a neuron feeds its output back to its own synaptic input, enabling intrinsic feedback modulation. The system integrates a solid electrolyte-based synaptic transistor capable of multiplexing multiple inputs and a bidirectional leaky integrate-and-fire artificial neuron. By feeding the neuronal output back to an additional synaptic gate, excitatory and inhibitory feedback loops are realized within a compact architecture. Using an artificial thermoregulation platform, temperature-dependent inputs bidirectionally modulate neuronal firing frequency, demonstrating biologically inspired feedback control with a compact set of neuromorphic devices for autonomous and energy-efficient systems.

title: Thin-film lithium niobate waveguide-integrated p-i-n Tungsten selenide photodiodes with 10Gbit/s data reception
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising photonic platform in next-generation integrated optoelectronics and on-chip/chip-chip interconnection due to its attractive optical property and versatility. However, integration of conventional-material-based photodetectors on TFLN platforms still faces multiple challenges. Herein, a high-bandwidth TFLN-based waveguide-integrated lateral WSe2 p-i-n photodetector is presented. The localized self-aligned doping process eliminates slow carrier diffusion and defect trapping in doped regions which further boosts modulation bandwidth. Secondly, n-type and p-type Ohmic contacts, along with a high-quality p-n junction, are achieved through Se vacancy defect engineering and high-work function molybdenum oxide buffer layer, respectively. Furthermore, combined with the high dielectric constant of lithium niobate suppressing ionized impurity scattering, carrier mobilities exceeding 350 cm2/V·s are achieved for both electrons and holes, significantly accelerating carrier drift. The device features a measured bandwidth of 1.12 GHz and a data rate up to 10 Gbit/s in visible light. Separately, the device achieves a responsivity of ~492 mA·W−1 and a near-unity external quantum efficiency of 95.6% at 638 nm. This combination of two-dimensional homostructure and TFLN nano-waveguides provides a basis for high-speed photodetectors and visible-light interconnections in future TFLN integrated optoelectronics and optical input/output applications.
